content.text:
The ledger is built, verified, and pushed. Three commits on `claude/genera-capability-ledger-d3ygam`.

## What's in the repo

`references/capabilities.yaml` is the source of truth (**42 rows**); `CAPABILITY_LEDGER.md` is generated by `scripts/gen_ledger.py` and committed so it reads without running anything. `--check` fails on staleness.

**15 SUPPORTED · 13 PARTIAL · 7 UNSUPPORTED · 4 UI_ONLY · 3 DRIFT**

## The three-commit structure gives you the verification delta for free

I kept Pass 1 snapshot-only (asserted it in code — evidence sources were exactly `{openapi_snapshot_2026_08_30}`) so `git diff ab1f6db 86be791` *is* the delta, not a recollection of one.

**Every live-docs correction went the same direction — the snapshot-only pass over-claimed that Ramp couldn't do things it can.** That's the failure mode the README grades explicitly.

- **`CAP-SCOPED-VISIBILITY` UNSUPPORTED → PARTIAL** — the significant one. Visibility follows the *reporting chain*, not department labels, and that's settable via `direct_manager_id`. The snapshot-only read saw `GET /roles` was read-only and concluded no surface existed. There is one; it just isn't the role enum. This would have wrongly flagged packet E's six district managers as unserviceable.
- **`CAP-APPROVAL-CHAIN` → UI_ONLY** — chains are real, built in Ramp's in-app workflow builder. "Ramp cannot do this" would have been wrong in all six packets, and the hand-to-deployment-owner workaround is now evidenced rather than assumed.
- **`CAP-ENTITY-CREATE` → UI_ONLY** — upgraded from absence-of-endpoint to a positive statement: *"Entities are created in the Ramp UI."*

Two corrections that didn't change a verdict but matter: `CAP-MCC-ALLOWLIST` stays UNSUPPORTED now on *positive* evidence (Ramp derives its own category from the MCC, so the UI can't express an allow-list either), and `DRIFT-LIMITS-FUNDS` now records that live docs still call the resource "spend limits" — so no audit log claims the API has no limits concept.

## Two things worth your attention

**I dropped a drift row the handoff planned.** It listed `permitted_spend_types` as drift (2 booleans vs 3). The snapshot has *both* shapes at different object levels — `ApiPermittedSpendTypesRequestBody` (spend programs) requires exactly `primary_card_enabled` + `reimbursements_enabled`, matching the exercise schema exactly; the 3-boolean shape belongs to funds. Not drift. I kept it as an explicit `NOT-DRIFT-SPEND-TYPES` row so no packet re-derives the wrong conclusion — asserting it would have put a false "the API moved on" claim in all five audit logs.

**The packet-A dry run paid off, as the plan predicted.** Two gaps, both recurring rather than A-specific: `CAP-ROLE-MAPPING` (title→role is a judgement call in every packet and had no row) and `CAP-IT-ADMIN-SCOPE`. The latter is the sharpest illustration of why live docs mattered — packet A wants Sana to "manage users but not change spend limits." The snapshot gives you the enum value `IT_ADMIN` and *nothing* about what it permits. The help centre says IT Admins edit People and Integrations but cannot manage spend controls. That's the ask exactly, as a stock role. Snapshot-only, I'd have reached for a custom role that isn't API-creatable and flagged it UNSUPPORTED.

## Notes on constraints

`docs.ramp.com` is blocked by org egress policy for both curl and WebFetch — **WebSearch was my only live channel**, so live-docs rows cite page titles and quoted snippets rather than full pages. Worth knowing before NOTES.md claims deeper doc reading than happened. I also verified the handoff's schema claims directly rather than trusting them; every one checked out.

I stopped at the ledger since that's what you scoped. Next per the plan: `SKILL.md`, then A → C → D. One thing to decide when you pick that up — whether `run_pipeline.py` is a real script or an instruction to a fresh session; the README allows either and it shapes how `SKILL.md` gets written.

You are building three small verification scripts for a Ramp deployment pipeline in the repo at /home/user/Genera. Work only in that repo.

# YOU OWN EXACTLY THESE THREE FILES — create no others, edit no others
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/scripts/check_quotes.py
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/scripts/check_coverage.py
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/scripts/lint_roster.py

Other agents are concurrently writing run_pipeline.py and the references/*.md files. Do NOT touch those, do NOT touch capabilities.yaml, gen_ledger.py, SKILL.md, or anything under candidate/. Do not git commit or push.

# CONTEXT

The pipeline ingests one "customer packet" (raw transcripts, rosters, Slack exports) and emits two JSON files that must validate against shipped schemas. An audit log is half the deliverable: it records assumptions, missing info, conflicts, and things the Ramp API cannot do.

Read these first to ground yourself:
- /home/user/Genera/README.md
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/references/capabilities.yaml  (the capability ledger, 42 rows — SOURCE OF TRUTH)
- /home/user/Genera/candidate/schemas/audit_log_schema.json
- /home/user/Genera/candidate/schemas/ramp_config_schema.json
- /home/user/Genera/candidate/customer_packets/client_a_acme_corp/  (a real packet; the roster CSV there is your lint_roster test case)

# DATA CONTRACTS (fixed — build to these exactly)

Ledger row fields in capabilities.yaml under top-level key `capabilities`:
  id, verdict (one of SUPPORTED|PARTIAL|UI_ONLY|UNSUPPORTED|DRIFT), title,
  customer_phrasings[], api_mechanism{endpoints[],fields[]},
  evidence[{source,checked_on,note}], evidence_line, config_expression{section,mechanism,note}, workaround, seen_in[]

work/<packet>/requirements.json:
{"packet": "client_a_acme_corp",
 "requirements": [
   {"req_id":"REQ-001","claim":"CEO card should effectively have no limit",
    "source_file":"discovery_call_01.txt",
    "source_quote":"I never want to see a decline",
    "archetype_id":"CAP-UNLIMITED","confidence":"high"}]}
 - source_quote is verbatim text captured at extraction time
 - archetype_id is a ledger row id, or null if nothing matched

work/<packet>/traceability.json:
{"packet": "client_a_acme_corp",
 "entries": [
   {"req_id":"REQ-001","archetype_id":"CAP-UNLIMITED","disposition":"both",
    "config_paths":["limits[3]"],"audit_refs":["assumptions_made[2]"]}]}
 - disposition is "config" | "audit" | "both"
 - config_paths are dotted/indexed paths into ramp_config.json
 - audit_refs are indexed paths into audit_log.json, e.g. "unsupported_api_requests[0]"

out/<packet>/ramp_config.json and out/<packet>/audit_log.json — only these two files in out/.

Packet source files live at candidate/customer_packets/<packet>/<source_file>.

# THE SCRIPTS

## 1. check_quotes.py
CLI: `python3 check_quotes.py --packet <packet_name>` (packet_name is the directory name, e.g. client_a_acme_corp)
Purpose: catch hallucinated citations. For every requirement in requirements.json, assert source_quote appears VERBATIM in candidate/customer_packets/<packet>/<source_file>.
- Normalize whitespace (collapse runs of whitespace to single spaces) on both sides before comparing, and normalize unicode quotes/dashes to ASCII equivalents — transcripts use curly quotes and em dashes, and an extractor may normalize them. Do NOT lowercase.
- Fail if source_file does not exist in the packet.
- On failure print the req_id, the source_file, and the first ~70 chars of the offending quote.
- Exit 0 if all quotes verify, 1 otherwise. Print a one-line summary either way ("N/N quotes verified").
Target ~45 lines.

## 2. check_coverage.py
CLI: `python3 check_coverage.py --packet <packet_name>`
Reads work/<packet>/requirements.json, work/<packet>/traceability.json, out/<packet>/audit_log.json, and the ledger.
Runs four checks, each a small named function, and reports ALL failures (do not stop at the first). Exit 1 if any fail.

  (a) COVERAGE INVARIANT — every req_id in requirements.json must have a traceability entry with at least one config_path or audit_ref. Orphans fail the run. Also fail on a traceability entry whose req_id is not in requirements.json.

  (b) FALSE-POSITIVE SWEEP — for every traceability entry whose audit_refs include an "unsupported_api_requests[...]" ref, look up its archetype_id in the ledger. If that row's verdict is SUPPORTED, FAIL. Rationale: claiming the API cannot do something it demonstrably can is explicitly graded. Entries with archetype_id null are skipped with a warning line (not a failure).

  (c) FALSE-NEGATIVE SWEEP — for every traceability entry that has config_paths but NO audit_refs, look up its archetype_id. If the verdict is UNSUPPORTED, UI_ONLY, or PARTIAL, FAIL: it has been silently configured as if fully supported, with nothing in the audit log. Verdicts SUPPORTED and DRIFT pass. archetype_id null → warning, not failure.

  (d) EVIDENCE COMPLETENESS — every entry in audit_log.json's unsupported_api_requests[] must have a non-empty `evidence` string containing a 4-digit year (a date), so evidence is always dated. Report the index of any that fail.

Print a compact pass/fail line per check plus details for failures, naming req_ids. This script may run to ~90 lines since it bundles four checks; keep each check its own function.

## 3. lint_roster.py
CLI: `python3 lint_roster.py <path-to-csv> [--json]`
Purpose: deterministic detection of roster dirt an LLM skims past. Produces findings that become conflicts/missing-info rows.
Detect, using heuristic column matching (case-insensitive substring on headers, so it works on unseen packets):
  - duplicate rows by email (report each email and the differing values across its rows — the point is to surface the disagreement, e.g. two different limits)
  - blank/empty cells in any detected limit column, and blank emails
  - non-numeric values in a limit column (e.g. "NO LIMIT")
  - case-variant / whitespace-variant values within a department-like column (e.g. "sales" vs "Sales") that would create duplicate departments
  - dangling manager references: a manager-email column value that is not itself an email in the roster (blank manager is fine — that is the top of the chain)
Column detection: find the header containing "email" (and not "manager") for identity; "manager" for manager refs; "depart" for department; "limit" for limits. If a column is absent, skip that check rather than crashing.
Output: human-readable summary by default; with --json emit a JSON object {"findings":[{"kind":...,"detail":...,"rows":[...]}]} to stdout.
Exit 0 ALWAYS (this is a reporting tool, not a gate) — but print a clear count of findings.
Target ~60 lines.

Verify it against candidate/customer_packets/client_a_acme_corp/department_roster.csv, which genuinely contains: a duplicated email with two different limits, a blank limit, a "NO LIMIT" string, lowercase "sales" alongside "Sales", and a manager email that appears nowhere as a roster member. Your script MUST find all five classes there. Report in your final message exactly what it found.

# GENERAL REQUIREMENTS
- Python 3, standard library only EXCEPT `yaml` (pyyaml is installed) for reading the ledger.
- Each script: a module docstring explaining what it catches and why that matters, and a `main()` returning an exit code, invoked via `if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main())`.
- Resolve repo paths relative to the script's own location (the scripts live at .claude/skills/ramp-deployment/scripts/, so the repo root is three parents up) — never rely on the caller's cwd.
- Make paths overridable with an optional `--repo` argument defaulting to that computed root.
- Legibility matters more than cleverness: a reviewer should understand each script in about a minute.
- Match the house style of the existing /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/scripts/gen_ledger.py — read it first and follow its conventions (docstring, constants, small functions, argparse-free simple sys.argv handling is fine if that is what it does).

# TESTING (required — do not skip)
You have no requirements.json or traceability.json to test against. CREATE TEMPORARY FIXTURES under /tmp to test check_quotes.py and check_coverage.py: build a small requirements.json/traceability.json/audit_log.json that exercises both the passing and the failing path of every check (including a deliberate false-positive and a deliberate false-negative), run the scripts with --repo pointed at your fixture tree, and confirm they pass and fail as intended. Do NOT leave fixtures inside /home/user/Genera — put them in /tmp. Delete nothing from the repo.

In your final message report: each script's line count, exactly what lint_roster.py found in the real packet A roster, and the results of your fixture tests for both the pass and fail paths of checks (a)-(d).

input.prompt:
You are writing three reference documents for a Ramp deployment pipeline skill in the repo at /home/user/Genera. Work only in that repo.

# YOU OWN EXACTLY THESE THREE FILES — create no others, edit no others
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/references/CATEGORY_MAP.md
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/references/PRECEDENCE_RULES.md
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/references/AUDIT_PATTERNS.md

Other agents are concurrently writing run_pipeline.py and the scripts/*.py files. Do NOT touch those. Do NOT touch capabilities.yaml, CAPABILITY_LEDGER.md, gen_ledger.py, SKILL.md, or anything under candidate/. Do not git commit or push.

# CONTEXT

The pipeline ingests one "customer packet" (raw transcripts, rosters, Slack exports, policy memos) and emits two JSON files: a desired-state ramp_config.json and an audit_log.json recording assumptions, missing information, conflicts, and requests the Ramp API cannot fulfil. The audit log is half the graded deliverable; a confidently wrong config is the worst outcome.

Read these first, they are essential grounding:
- /home/user/Genera/README.md
- /home/user/Genera/candidate/README.md  (the exercise spec — source of truth for direction)
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/references/capabilities.yaml  (42-row capability ledger, SOURCE OF TRUTH for what Ramp can do)
- /home/user/Genera/candidate/schemas/ramp_config_schema.json and audit_log_schema.json
- /home/user/Genera/candidate/sample_packet/client_0_sample_westbrook/  (a worked example WITH finished output in example_output/ — study its idioms closely)
- All five packets under /home/user/Genera/candidate/customer_packets/

These docs are read by a fresh Claude Code session mid-run. Write them to be *used*, not admired: scannable, specific, and short enough to load without burning context. Prefer tables and short bullets over prose. No preamble, no filler.

# 1. CATEGORY_MAP.md — MCC to Ramp category translation

Ramp does NOT support allow-listing at raw MCC granularity (see ledger row CAP-MCC-ALLOWLIST). It restricts on its own vocabulary of 44 integer category codes. Every MCC-to-category translation is therefore lossy and must be logged.

REQUIRED FIRST STEP: extract the REAL category vocabulary from the OpenAPI snapshot at
/home/user/Genera/candidate/2026_08_30_Ramp_OpenAPI_Schema.json (2.3 MB, JSON).
The 44 codes (1-44, with no 22) and their names are in there — find them by searching the schema components for the category code enum/description. Known anchors to confirm you found the right thing: 4 = Airlines, 6 = Lodging, 18 = Fuel and gas, 19 = Restaurants, 20 = Alcohol and bars, 40 = SaaS / Software. Do NOT invent or guess names — if you cannot find a code's name in the snapshot, mark it explicitly as not-found rather than filling it in.

The document must contain:
- The full authoritative table of the 44 Ramp category codes and names, as extracted.
- A translation table mapping common MCC codes and MCC ranges to the nearest Ramp category, with a LOSSY column (exact / narrower / broader / no representation) and a note for each lossy one.
- Explicit handling of MCC *ranges*: packet E's matrix uses `3000-3299`, which is the airline range in Amex reporting. Ramp has no range concept and no per-MCC allow-list, so it collapses to category 4 (Airlines). Say plainly what is lost.
- A short "how to use this" section: for each row in a customer MCC matrix, emit the Ramp category, and write a `translation_notes` string for the mcc_controls entry plus an assumptions_made entry when the mapping is not exact.
- A warning that `blocked_mcc_codes` DOES exist for blocking (write-only — settable on request bodies, absent from response schemas), so blocking specific MCCs is possible even though allow-listing is not. Do not let a reader conclude MCCs are entirely unusable.

Cross-check your claims against ledger rows CAP-MCC-ALLOWLIST, CAP-MCC-BLOCKLIST, CAP-CATEGORY-RESTRICT and reuse their evidence_line strings where relevant.

# 2. PRECEDENCE_RULES.md — how conflicts resolve, per packet

Conflicts must be LOGGED even when a stated rule resolves them. The audit schema says: "Do not silently pick a winner — record both, say which you provisionally encoded and why." A stated precedence rule goes in `provisional_resolution`; it does NOT suppress the conflict entry. Make this the document's opening principle.

For each packet A-E, read the actual source files and record:
- every stated precedence rule, quoted VERBATIM with its location (timestamp, section number, or line context)
- what it resolves and what it does NOT resolve
- any conflict that must be flagged `blocking: true` rather than resolved

Specific things you must find, verify verbatim in the files, and record precisely (these are known to exist — confirm the exact wording and location yourself rather than trusting this summary):
- Packet A: a stated rule that the roster wins over anything said on the call, around timestamp 04:31. Note that it resolves per-person limit numbers but does NOT resolve the Marketing reorg question, which the same speaker explicitly says not to invent an answer to.
- Packet B: memo section 5.3 resolves language-version discrepancies in favour of the SPANISH version, EXCEPT Section 4 (Miami) whose original is English. Plus a second, spoken precedence rule where the CFO says the memo is aspirational about eliminating reimbursements and to follow the operations director instead — operation beats memo. Both need verbatim quotes.
- Packet D: the travel-approval conflict between the February notes (tiered, under $2,500 auto-approved) and a later Slack message from Leo demanding ALL travel come to him. The later source is more recent, but the earlier one documents an agreement and the note-taker explicitly flags they were not in the meeting and cannot find confirmation the trial was cancelled. This must be flagged BLOCKING, not silently resolved by recency. ---
name: ramp-deployment
description: Turn a raw customer packet (call transcripts, rosters, Slack exports, policy memos) into a desired-state ramp_config.json plus an audit_log.json that records every assumption, gap, conflict, and unsupported request. Use when asked to run a customer packet, produce a Ramp deployment config, or build the two graded JSON outputs.

# Ramp deployment: packet to config

You are doing a deployment rep's first pass. A customer's messy reality goes in; a
concrete Ramp configuration and an honest audit trail come out.

**The audit log is half the deliverable.** A deployment rep trusts the config exactly as
far as the audit log is honest. A confidently wrong config is the worst possible outcome —
worse than an incomplete one. When in doubt, flag it.

## Run it

```
python3 run_pipeline.py --packet client_a_acme_corp     # Phase 0: setup + runbook
python3 run_pipeline.py --packet client_a_acme_corp --verify   # Phase 4: all checks
```

Phase 0 and Phase 4 are mechanical and scripted. **Phases 1-3 are yours** — the judgement
work is the job, and it does not automate.

## The one invariant

> Every requirement extracted in Phase 1 must terminate in a config field, an audit entry,
> or both. Nothing is dropped silently.

Phase 4 fails the run on any orphan. This is what makes "flag-forward" mechanically true
rather than aspirational.

## Files you will use

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `references/capabilities.yaml` | **The capability ledger — 42 rows, source of truth for what Ramp can do.** Read it before deciding anything is impossible. |
| `references/CAPABILITY_LEDGER.md` | Same content, readable. Generated — never edit it. |
| `references/AUDIT_PATTERNS.md` | The four trigger classes. The engine of Phase 2. |
| `references/PRECEDENCE_RULES.md` | How conflicts resolve, per packet, with verbatim quotes. |
| `references/CATEGORY_MAP.md` | MCC to Ramp's 44 categories. Every mapping is lossy; log it. |
| `candidate/schemas/*.json` | The submission contract. `additionalProperties: false` throughout **both** files. |
| `candidate/sample_packet/.../example_output/` | Worked example. Study its idioms before writing anything. |

---

# Phase 1 — Extract

Read **every** file in the packet. Not a skim: the dirt is in the details, and packets are
deliberately built so the important things sit in asides.

Write `work/<packet>/requirements.json`:

```json
{"packet": "client_a_acme_corp",
 "requirements": [
   {"req_id": "REQ-001",
    "claim": "CEO's card should effectively have no limit",
    "source_file": "discovery_call_01.txt",
    "source_quote": "I never want to see a decline",
    "archetype_id": "CAP-UNLIMITED",
    "confidence": "high"}]}
```

**Capture every quote verbatim, at extraction time.** Copy it out of the file as you read.
Reconstructing a quote later from memory is exactly how citations get hallucinated, and
Phase 4 checks every one of them against the file with a substring match. The audit schema
wants "file + line/quote"; this is where you earn it.

Tag each requirement with the closest ledger `archetype_id`, or `null` if nothing fits.
A `null` is a signal, not a failure — it means the ledger may need a new row. Say so.

If the packet has a roster CSV, run the linter before you trust it:

```
python3 .claude/skills/ramp-deployment/scripts/lint_roster.py <path-to-csv>
```

It deterministically finds duplicate emails with disagreeing values, blank cells,
non-numeric limits, case-variant department names, and dangling manager references. These
become `conflicts` and `missing_information_flags` rows. An LLM reading a 33-row CSV will
skim past all five classes; the script will not.

---

# Phase 2 — Flag

**Write the audit log before the config exists.** This ordering is deliberate: if you
compose first, the audit log becomes a rationalization of what you already built. Flagging
first makes composition downstream of the flags.

Write `out/<packet>/audit_log.json`. Four trigger classes, each feeding one array — the
full taxonomy with worked examples is in `references/AUDIT_PATTERNS.md`. In brief:

| Array | Fires on |
|---|---|
| `assumptions_made` | any value not literally stated; inference from headcount; role mapping; currency normalization; MCC translation; group fan-out; rounding; every `UI_ONLY` capability you omitted |
| `missing_information_flags` | named person without an email; a document referenced but absent; headcount with no roster; unresolvable manager; anything a source says is "coming" |
| `conflicts` | same field, two values; a source contradicting itself; supersession by time |
| `unsupported_api_requests` | any requirement whose ledger verdict is not `SUPPORTED` |

Three rules that matter more than the rest:

1. **A stated precedence rule does not suppress a conflict.** The schema is explicit: "Do
   not silently pick a winner — record both, say which you provisionally encoded and why."
   The rule goes in `provisional_resolution`. The conflict still gets logged.
2. **Copy `evidence` verbatim from the ledger row's `evidence_line`.** Never compose it
   fresh. That is how several audit logs stay consistent with each other instead of each
   re-arguing the same point. `proposed_manual_workaround` comes from the row's `workaround`.
3. **Do not list things the API supports.** Getting `unsupported_api_requests` right
   *including not over-listing* is explicitly graded. Check the ledger verdict before you
   claim anything is impossible — several verdicts that look like gaps are `UI_ONLY`
   (real capability, wrong surface) or `PARTIAL` (possible with a caveat).

> "An empty audit log on a messy packet is a red flag, not an achievement."

---

# Phase 3 — Compose

Write `out/<packet>/ramp_config.json`, walking the eight sections in schema order:
`entities, departments, locations, users, spend_programs, limits, approval_policies,
mcc_controls`.

Consult the ledger per requirement. What a verdict means for where the requirement lands:

| Verdict | In the config? | In the audit log? |
|---|---|---|
| `SUPPORTED` | yes | only if you inferred a value |
| `PARTIAL` | yes | **always** — `unsupported_api_requests`, naming the caveat |
| `UI_ONLY` | yes if the schema has a home; otherwise omit | **always** |
| `UNSUPPORTED` | yes if the schema has a home; otherwise omit | **always** |
| `DRIFT` | emit the **schema** shape, not the live API's | **always** — once per packet is enough |

`UNSUPPORTED` and `UI_ONLY` items still belong in the config as desired state wherever the
schema has somewhere to put them — the schema descriptions for `entities` and
`approval_policies` explicitly invite exactly this. Where there is no home (receipt
thresholds, memo rules), they live only in the audit log. That omit-and-flag move is the
idiom the Westbrook sample demonstrates with its $50 receipt rule.

Then write `work/<packet>/traceability.json`, linking every requirement to where it landed:

```json
{"packet": "client_a_acme_corp",
 "entries": [
   {"req_id": "REQ-001", "archetype_id": "CAP-UNLIMITED", "disposition": "both",
    "config_paths": ["limits[3]"], "audit_refs": ["assumptions_made[2]"]}]}
```

This file is how Phase 4 proves the coverage invariant and runs both graded sweeps. It
lives in `work/` because both output schemas set `additionalProperties: false`, so there is
nowhere in `out/` to carry the linkage.

## Schema traps

These will bite. The validator catches none of them.

- **`limits[].assigned_to`** — the description says exactly one of `user_email` or `group`
  must be set, but there is **no `oneOf`**, so nothing enforces it. `--verify` checks it.
- **`threshold_usd_cents` is USD by field name.** A packet quoting approval thresholds in
  MXN or BRL creates a real tension. That needs an audit entry, not a silent conversion.
- **Six roles, no `BUSINESS_OWNER`.** Map owners to `BUSINESS_ADMIN` and log the mapping.
- **No `allowed_mcc_codes` mechanism** — the enum has `blocked_mcc_codes` but allow-listing
  exists only at category granularity. See `CATEGORY_MAP.md`.
- **Seven intervals, no `TERTIARY`.** The live API has eight.
- **`permitted_spend_types` takes exactly two booleans** and forbids anything else.
- `out/` contains **only** the two JSON files. Intermediates go in `work/`.

---

# Phase 4 — Verify

```
python3 run_pipeline.py --packet <packet> --verify
```

Six checks, in order: outputs parse; both files validate against the shipped schemas; every
quote matches its source file; the coverage invariant plus both graded sweeps; the
`assigned_to` exactly-one rule; ledger freshness.

The two sweeps are the ones the exercise grades explicitly, in **both** directions:

- **False-positive sweep** — nothing sits in `unsupported_api_requests` that the ledger
  marks `SUPPORTED`. Claiming Ramp cannot do something it can is a failure mode, and it is
  the one candidates miss.
- **False-negative sweep** — nothing is configured as if fully supported when the ledger
  says `UNSUPPORTED`, `UI_ONLY`, or `PARTIAL` and the audit log says nothing about it.

Fix what it reports and run it again. Green is the bar.

---

# Working notes

**If the ledger is wrong, fix the ledger.** When a packet reveals a capability question no
row answers, add the row to `references/capabilities.yaml`, regenerate with
`scripts/gen_ledger.py`, and commit that separately. The ledger is the reusable asset here —
it is what makes the next packet cheaper, including one nobody has seen. A `null`
`archetype_id` in Phase 1 is the signal.

**Evidence beats absence.** "This endpoint isn't in the OpenAPI snapshot" is weak evidence
that Ramp cannot do something — it may be a UI capability, or a renamed path. Three ledger
verdicts were corrected on exactly this point. Where a claim is load-bearing, corroborate it
against the live docs before the audit log asserts it, and cite what you checked and when.

**Script budget.** If a check cannot be written in about 40 lines, it becomes an instruction
here instead of a script. The deliverable is instructions plus small scripts; anything that
smells like infrastructure is out of scope.

**Time discipline.** Packets A, C and D are the core. If you are running over, cut E, then
B. Never cut the audit logs.

                     nothing claimed impossible that the ledger says is SUPPORTED;
                     false negative: nothing silently configured when the ledger says
                     UNSUPPORTED/UI_ONLY/PARTIAL and the audit log is silent) plus
                     evidence-dating.
  lint_roster.py     deterministic roster dirt. Verified against packet A: finds all
                     five real classes — duplicate email with disagreeing limits,

    __file__ so they run from any cwd.

content.content:
# CATEGORY_MAP.md — MCC to Ramp category translation

Ramp does not restrict on raw MCCs in the allow direction. It restricts on its own
category vocabulary. Every MCC allow-list a customer hands you is therefore translated,
every translation is lossy, and every lossy translation is logged.

## The three facts that govern this document

| Fact | Ledger row | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| You cannot allow-list at raw MCC granularity — anywhere, API or UI | `CAP-MCC-ALLOWLIST` | UNSUPPORTED |
| You **can** block specific MCCs — write-only, no read-back | `CAP-MCC-BLOCKLIST` | PARTIAL |
| You can allow/block on Ramp's integer category codes | `CAP-CATEGORY-RESTRICT` | SUPPORTED |

Evidence strings to copy verbatim into `unsupported_api_requests[].evidence`:

# AUDIT_PATTERNS.md — trigger taxonomy and idioms

The engine of Phase 2. Four trigger classes, four arrays, no fifth place to put anything.

> "An empty audit log on a messy packet is a red flag, not an achievement."
> — `candidate/schemas/audit_log_schema.json`, top-level `description`

## Routing

| Class | Array | One-line test |
|---|---|---|
| Judgement | `assumptions_made` | I chose a value the customer did not state |
| Gap | `missing_information_flags` | I needed something the packet does not contain |
| Disagreement | `conflicts` | Two sources — or one source twice — say different things |
| Capability | `unsupported_api_requests` | The ledger verdict for this requirement is not `SUPPORTED` |

**One requirement can fire several classes.** Acme's CEO card fires all four: an assumption
($50,000 is the invented ceiling), a conflict (roster "NO LIMIT" vs the call's "$50k"), a
capability entry (`CAP-UNLIMITED`), and arguably a gap (is $50k the number Marcus expects?).
Do not pick one. Firing once is the most common way an audit log goes thin.

**Every array is required by the schema**, and `additionalProperties: false` applies
everywhere. Empty arrays are legal — see the Westbrook idioms — but an empty array is a
claim you are making, not a default.

---

## 1. `assumptions_made`

Judgement calls a human could veto.

### Fires on

| Trigger | Typical packet |
|---|---|
| Any value in the config not literally stated in a source | all |
| Headcount → individual people ("about a dozen", "roughly 40 eng") | A, B, D, E |
| Role mapping where customer language has no clean Ramp enum (`CAP-ROLE-MAPPING`) | all |
| Currency normalization, and any FX rate you picked | B |
| MCC → Ramp category translation, once per lossy mapping (`CAP-MCC-ALLOWLIST`) | C, E |
| Group limit fanned out to per-user limits (`CAP-GROUP-LIMIT`) | A, D, E |
| Any rounding — "equivalent, not identical" amounts, cents conversion | B |
| **Every `UI_ONLY` capability you left out of the config** — omitting it *is* an assumption | all |
| Normalizing case-variant or near-duplicate labels (`sales` vs `Sales`) | A |

### Required fields

`assumption` · `source` (file + line or quote) · `impact_if_wrong`. Nothing else is allowed.

`impact_if_wrong` is the field that gets skimped. Write the consequence in the world — who
can spend what, who sees what — not "the config would be incorrect".

### Worked example — UI_ONLY omission (packet A)

Priya Shetty: "Required over seventy-five dollars. Below that I don't want anyone's time
spent on it. And memo required for anything over five hundred."

The skill is built, verified end-to-end, and pushed. **652 lines of Python, 240 lines of SKILL.md, three reference docs.**

## How the fan-out went

I pinned the data contracts (`requirements.json`, `traceability.json`, and each script's CLI) *before* spawning, and gave each agent disjoint file ownership. That paid off — the three outputs composed with no rework, and the `run_pipeline.py` agent independently confirmed it by building a sandbox fixture that passed through the sibling scripts it had never seen.

## What the agents caught that I'd have shipped wrong

Two were genuine saves:

- **The date regex.** My contract said "evidence must contain a 4-digit year," which naturally becomes `\b\d{4}\b`. Word boundaries don't fire before an underscore — so that pattern rejects `openapi snapshot 2026_08_30`, i.e. **every evidence line in the ledger**. Verified: naive pattern `False`, corrected pattern `True`.
- **Path resolution.** My brief said the repo root was three parents up from `scripts/`; it's four. Corrected and verified by running from `/`.

The references agent also independently counted the category vocabulary and found **43 codes, not 44** — 1–44 with 22 absent. The handoff's "44 integer codes (1–44, no 22)" is self-contradictory, and my ledger had inherited it in four places. Two independent derivations agreeing made that an easy fix.

## What I found by testing rather than trusting

**The coverage invariant was hollow.** I built a smoke fixture from the Westbrook sample's real outputs and real email quotes, and `check_coverage` passed — while citing `assumptions_made[999]` against an audit log with one entry. Nothing resolved citations against the actual document, so "every requirement lands somewhere" was satisfiable by pointing at nothing. I added check (e); it immediately caught three dangling refs, two of which I'd written myself without noticing. I then confirmed the other sweeps aren't vacuous — deliberately filing a `SUPPORTED` capability as unsupported fires the false-positive sweep, and configuring a `UI_ONLY` one with no audit trace fires the false-negative sweep.

Two smaller finds: the config takes category **name strings** (`"Software / SaaS"`) while the API takes integer codes — emitting codes validates cleanly and is wrong. And `source_quote` must be a **contiguous span**, since `check_quotes` does substring matching and an elided quote fails even when honest. Both are now documented traps in SKILL.md.

## One thing you should know

**The references agent hit your session rate limit and died mid-sentence — during its own final validation of the JSON snippets and ledger-verbatim strings.** Its files were complete but self-unverified, so I redid that check directly: every JSON snippet parses, every ledger row id resolves, every quoted evidence line is verbatim (one exception is explicitly labelled as the sample's line shown as a format example), and 31/39 quoted fragments in `PRECEDENCE_RULES.md` matched a packet file verbatim. I chased all eight misses to source — every one was a checker artifact (ellipsis, markdown bold, a nested quotation), not a fabrication.

Worth noting the limit resets at 10:10pm UTC in case it constrains the packet runs.

## State

No packet has been run yet — `out/` is empty, which is correct. Next is A → C → D end-to-end, then `NOTES.md`. The verification delta section already has three strong entries banked from this session's git history: the three corrected ledger verdicts, the 43-vs-44 count, and the hollow coverage invariant.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment

# Ramp deployment: packet to config

You are doing a deployment rep's first pass. A customer's messy reality goes in; a
concrete Ramp configuration and an honest audit trail come out.

**The audit log is half the deliverable.** A deployment rep trusts the config exactly as
far as the audit log is honest. A confidently wrong config is the worst possible outcome —
worse than an incomplete one. When in doubt, flag it.

## Run it

```
python3 run_pipeline.py --packet client_a_acme_corp     # Phase 0: setup + runbook
python3 run_pipeline.py --packet client_a_acme_corp --verify   # Phase 4: all checks
```

Phase 0 and Phase 4 are mechanical and scripted. **Phases 1-3 are yours** — the judgement
work is the job, and it does not automate.

## The one invariant

> Every requirement extracted in Phase 1 must terminate in a config field, an audit entry,
> or both. Nothing is dropped silently.

Phase 4 fails the run on any orphan. This is what makes "flag-forward" mechanically true
rather than aspirational.

## Files you will use

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `references/capabilities.yaml` | **The capability ledger — 42 rows, source of truth for what Ramp can do.** Read it before deciding anything is impossible. |
| `references/CAPABILITY_LEDGER.md` | Same content, readable. Generated — never edit it. |
| `references/AUDIT_PATTERNS.md` | The four trigger classes. The engine of Phase 2. |
| `references/PRECEDENCE_RULES.md` | How conflicts resolve, per packet, with verbatim quotes. |
| `references/CATEGORY_MAP.md` | MCC to Ramp's 43 category codes. Every mapping is lossy; log it. |
| `candidate/schemas/*.json` | The submission contract. `additionalProperties: false` throughout **both** files. |
| `candidate/sample_packet/.../example_output/` | Worked example. Study its idioms before writing anything. |

---

# Phase 1 — Extract

Read **every** file in the packet. Not a skim: the dirt is in the details, and packets are
deliberately built so the important things sit in asides.

Write `work/<packet>/requirements.json`:

```json
{"packet": "client_a_acme_corp",
 "requirements": [
   {"req_id": "REQ-001",
    "claim": "CEO's card should effectively have no limit",
    "source_file": "discovery_call_01.txt",
    "source_quote": "I never want to see a decline",
    "archetype_id": "CAP-UNLIMITED",
    "confidence": "high"}]}
```

**Capture every quote verbatim, at extraction time.** Copy it out of the file as you read.
Reconstructing a quote later from memory is exactly how citations get hallucinated, and
Phase 4 checks every one of them against the file with a substring match. The audit schema
wants "file + line/quote"; this is where you earn it.

`source_quote` must be a **contiguous span** — no `...` elision, no stitching two sentences
together. The check is a substring match after whitespace and unicode-punctuation
normalization, so an elided quote fails even when it is honest. If the useful material spans
a gap, either quote the shorter contiguous piece or split it into two requirements. (Prose in
`NOTES.md` and the reference docs may elide freely; this rule is only about
`requirements.json`.)

Tag each requirement with the closest ledger `archetype_id`, or `null` if nothing fits.
A `null` is a signal, not a failure — it means the ledger may need a new row. Say so.

If the packet has a roster CSV, run the linter before you trust it:

```
python3 .claude/skills/ramp-deployment/scripts/lint_roster.py <path-to-csv>
```

It deterministically finds duplicate emails with disagreeing values, blank cells,
non-numeric limits, case-variant department names, and dangling manager references. These
become `conflicts` and `missing_information_flags` rows. An LLM reading a 33-row CSV will
skim past all five classes; the script will not.

---

# Phase 2 — Flag

**Write the audit log before the config exists.** This ordering is deliberate: if you
compose first, the audit log becomes a rationalization of what you already built. Flagging
first makes composition downstream of the flags.

Write `out/<packet>/audit_log.json`. Four trigger classes, each feeding one array — the
full taxonomy with worked examples is in `references/AUDIT_PATTERNS.md`. In brief:

| Array | Fires on |
|---|---|
| `assumptions_made` | any value not literally stated; inference from headcount; role mapping; currency normalization; MCC translation; group fan-out; rounding; every `UI_ONLY` capability you omitted |
| `missing_information_flags` | named person without an email; a document referenced but absent; headcount with no roster; unresolvable manager; anything a source says is "coming" |
| `conflicts` | same field, two values; a source contradicting itself; supersession by time |
| `unsupported_api_requests` | any requirement whose ledger verdict is not `SUPPORTED` |

Three rules that matter more than the rest:

1. **A stated precedence rule does not suppress a conflict.** The schema is explicit: "Do
   not silently pick a winner — record both, say which you provisionally encoded and why."
   The rule goes in `provisional_resolution`. The conflict still gets logged.
2. **Copy `evidence` verbatim from the ledger row's `evidence_line`.** Never compose it
   fresh. That is how several audit logs stay consistent with each other instead of each
   re-arguing the same point. `proposed_manual_workaround` comes from the row's `workaround`.
3. **Do not list things the API supports.** Getting `unsupported_api_requests` right
   *including not over-listing* is explicitly graded. Check the ledger verdict before you
   claim anything is impossible — several verdicts that look like gaps are `UI_ONLY`
   (real capability, wrong surface) or `PARTIAL` (possible with a caveat).

> "An empty audit log on a messy packet is a red flag, not an achievement."

---

# Phase 3 — Compose

Write `out/<packet>/ramp_config.json`, walking the eight sections in schema order:
`entities, departments, locations, users, spend_programs, limits, approval_policies,
mcc_controls`.

Consult the ledger per requirement. What a verdict means for where the requirement lands:

| Verdict | In the config? | In the audit log? |
|---|---|---|
| `SUPPORTED` | yes | only if you inferred a value |
| `PARTIAL` | yes | **always** — `unsupported_api_requests`, naming the caveat |
| `UI_ONLY` | yes if the schema has a home; otherwise omit | **always** |
| `UNSUPPORTED` | yes if the schema has a home; otherwise omit | **always** |
| `DRIFT` | emit the **schema** shape, not the live API's | **always** — once per packet is enough |

`UNSUPPORTED` and `UI_ONLY` items still belong in the config as desired state wherever the
schema has somewhere to put them — the schema descriptions for `entities` and
`approval_policies` explicitly invite exactly this. Where there is no home (receipt
thresholds, memo rules), they live only in the audit log. That omit-and-flag move is the
idiom the Westbrook sample demonstrates with its $50 receipt rule.

Then write `work/<packet>/traceability.json`, linking every requirement to where it landed:

```json
{"packet": "client_a_acme_corp",
 "entries": [
   {"req_id": "REQ-001", "archetype_id": "CAP-UNLIMITED", "disposition": "both",
    "config_paths": ["limits[3]"], "audit_refs": ["assumptions_made[2]"]}]}
```

This file is how Phase 4 proves the coverage invariant and runs both graded sweeps. It
lives in `work/` because both output schemas set `additionalProperties: false`, so there is
nowhere in `out/` to carry the linkage.

## Idioms worth copying from the sample

Read `candidate/sample_packet/.../example_output/ramp_config.json` before composing. It is
short and every line of it is a decision:

- `approval_policies[].source` carries the **verbatim quote** the policy came from
  (`"intake_email.txt — 'Anything over client_a_acme_corp,000 needs Priti's approval.'"`). Use it; it is
  where a reviewer looks when sources conflict.
- A tier list starts at `{"threshold_usd_cents": 0, "approver": "AUTO"}` — the auto-approve
  floor is an explicit tier, not an absence.
- A group limit says the fan-out in `notes`: *"One per Studio member (9 people) once the
  roster arrives."* Never leave a group limit's cardinality implicit.
- An unknown surname is encoded `"(surname pending roster)"` and paired with a **blocking**
  missing-information flag, rather than invented or left blank.
- `mcc_controls[].applies_to` is a limit or spend-program `display_name` — it must match one
  you actually emitted.

## Schema traps

These will bite. The validator catches none of them.

- **`limits[].assigned_to`** — the description says exactly one of `user_email` or `group`
  must be set, but there is **no `oneOf`**, so nothing enforces it. `--verify` checks it.
- **`threshold_usd_cents` is USD by field name.** A packet quoting approval thresholds in
  MXN or BRL creates a real tension. That needs an audit entry, not a silent conversion.
- **Six roles, no `BUSINESS_OWNER`.** Map owners to `BUSINESS_ADMIN` and log the mapping.
- **No `allowed_mcc_codes` mechanism** — the enum has `blocked_mcc_codes` but allow-listing
  exists only at category granularity. See `CATEGORY_MAP.md`.
- **Categories are name strings here, integer codes in the API.** `allowed_categories` is
  `array<string>` in this schema and the sample writes `"Software / SaaS"` — but the live API
  takes integer codes (`40`) on `allowed_category_codes`. Emit the **name**; record the code
  in `translation_notes` so the mapping survives into deployment. Getting this backwards
  validates cleanly and is wrong.
- **Seven intervals, no `TERTIARY`.** The live API has eight.
- **`permitted_spend_types` takes exactly two booleans** and forbids anything else.
- `out/` contains **only** the two JSON files. Intermediates go in `work/`.

---

# Phase 4 — Verify

```
python3 run_pipeline.py --packet <packet> --verify
```

Six checks, in order: outputs parse; both files validate against the shipped schemas; every
quote matches its source file; the coverage invariant plus both graded sweeps; the
`assigned_to` exactly-one rule; ledger freshness.

The two sweeps are the ones the exercise grades explicitly, in **both** directions:

- **False-positive sweep** — nothing sits in `unsupported_api_requests` that the ledger
  marks `SUPPORTED`. Claiming Ramp cannot do something it can is a failure mode, and it is
  the one candidates miss.
- **False-negative sweep** — nothing is configured as if fully supported when the ledger
  says `UNSUPPORTED`, `UI_ONLY`, or `PARTIAL` and the audit log says nothing about it.

Fix what it reports and run it again. Green is the bar.

---

# Working notes

**If the ledger is wrong, fix the ledger.** When a packet reveals a capability question no
row answers, add the row to `references/capabilities.yaml`, regenerate with
`scripts/gen_ledger.py`, and commit that separately. The ledger is the reusable asset here —
it is what makes the next packet cheaper, including one nobody has seen. A `null`
`archetype_id` in Phase 1 is the signal.

**Evidence beats absence.** "This endpoint isn't in the OpenAPI snapshot" is weak evidence
that Ramp cannot do something — it may be a UI capability, or a renamed path. Three ledger
verdicts were corrected on exactly this point. Where a claim is load-bearing, corroborate it
against the live docs before the audit log asserts it, and cite what you checked and when.

**Script budget.** If a check cannot be written in about 40 lines, it becomes an instruction
here instead of a script. The deliverable is instructions plus small scripts; anything that
smells like infrastructure is out of scope.

**Time discipline.** Packets A, C and D are the core. If you are running over, cut E, then
B. Never cut the audit logs.
Noting a defect immediately: the skill's arg substitution replaced `$1` in `$1,000` with the packet name. I'll fix that. First, Phase 0.

content.text:
Packet A is done — **7/7 checks green**, both files validating, pushed.

## Output

`out/client_a_acme_corp/` — 31 users, 5 departments, 2 spend programs, 31 limits, 2 approval policies, 2 MCC controls.

The audit log is **17 assumptions, 10 missing-information flags (5 blocking), 5 conflicts, 11 unsupported requests**. All 37 extracted requirements terminate somewhere; 37/37 quotes verified verbatim on the first pass.

## The packet's traps, and what happened to each

All five roster dirt classes were caught by `lint_roster.py` before I read the CSV, and each became a specific entry rather than a silent fix:

- **Han Zhao's duplicate rows** ($500 vs $1,200) — encoded $1,200 with a conflict entry that says plainly the roster-wins rule *can't arbitrate a roster disagreeing with itself*, so row order is the only tiebreak. Blocking.
- **Marcus's `NO LIMIT`** — the stated precedence rule doesn't resolve this either, because "NO LIMIT" isn't representable at all. Encoded Diane's own $50k figure, flagged for his confirmation.
- **Sam Whitfield's blank limit** — no limit emitted, blocking flag. He's in `users` with no card rather than given an invented number.
- **`sales`/`Sales`** — normalized, logged.
- **Jenny Park → `dkim@acme.example`** — `direct_manager_email: null`, blocking flag.

The Marketing reorg is flagged **non-blocking**, per Priya's explicit "don't block on it, but don't invent an answer either."

## Two defects the run exposed

**My own case-normalizer had the same bug the packet was testing for.** `.title()` turned `IT` into `It`, orphaning Sana from the `IT` department the config creates. Both are valid strings — schema validation passed clean. I added `--verify` check 6 (every department, program, limit and manager name must resolve to something emitted) and proved it fires by re-injecting that exact bug plus a typo'd program reference.

**Optional-but-typed fields can't be nulled** — `affected_config` is optional but typed `string`; `null` failed validation.

Both are now documented traps in SKILL.md. I also found and fixed a `$1` in SKILL.md being eaten by skill argument substitution — it corrupted the quoted sample into `Anything over client_a_acme_corp,000` when the skill loaded.

## One thing worth your judgement

The **new-vendor approval** is the weakest part of the config. Diane wants any new software vendor to need her sign-off "regardless of amount," but `tiers[]` is keyed only on `threshold_usd_cents` — so I encoded it as a zero-threshold tier on the Software program, which catches *all* software spend, not just new vendors. It's in the config with the over-capture stated in both the `source` field and the audit log, but it's a real semantic mismatch rather than a faithful encoding. Worth a sentence in NOTES.md.

The ledger gained `CAP-USER-LIMIT` (43 rows) — running a real packet showed the single most common request in the whole set had no row, because the ledger was written around the hard cases.

Ready for C next, which should go faster now that the checks are sharper.

The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.

# YOU OWN EXACTLY ONE FILE
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/scripts/check_audit_style.py

Do NOT create or edit anything else. Other agents and the parent are concurrently editing capabilities.yaml, SKILL.md, run_pipeline.py and AUDIT_PATTERNS.md. Do not git commit or push.

# BACKGROUND

The pipeline emits `out/<packet>/audit_log.json`. **That file is read by the customer** — for packet A, by Acme Corp's finance team. A customer reviewed the first one and raised three defects. Your script makes those defects impossible to ship again, on any packet.

Read first:
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/scripts/check_quotes.py  (house style — match it: shebang, module docstring with usage, module constants, small functions, plain sys.argv handling via an `arg()` helper, `main()` returning an exit code, `sys.exit(main())`)
- /home/user/Genera/.claude/skills/ramp-deployment/scripts/check_coverage.py (the multi-check reporting pattern — copy its "run every check, report all failures, PASS/FAIL line per check" structure)
- /home/user/Genera/out/client_a_acme_corp/audit_log.json  (a real audit log, currently violating all three rules)
- /home/user/Genera/candidate/schemas/audit_log_schema.json
- /home/user/Genera/candidate/customer_packets/client_a_acme_corp/  (the packet the audit log cites)

IMPORTANT: the repo root is `parents[4]` from the scripts directory (scripts -> ramp-deployment -> skills -> .claude -> root). Resolve paths from `__file__`, never cwd, and support an optional `--repo` override. CLI must be:

    python3 check_audit_style.py --packet <packet_name> [--repo <path>]

Exit 0 if every check passes, 1 otherwise. Report ALL failures, not just the first.

# THE CHECKS

## (a) No third-person pronouns
Scan every string value in all four audit arrays. Fail on any of: he, she, his, her, hers, him, they, them, their, theirs — whole word, case-insensitive.

The customer's rule: always reference a person by name or role, never by pronoun, because the audit log is customer-facing and pronouns make it ambiguous who is meant.

CRITICAL EXCEPTION: the `source` field of an entry legitimately contains a VERBATIM QUOTE from the customer's own documents, and the customer's own words may contain pronouns. You must not force a quote to be misquoted. So: within a `source` value, ignore any text inside single or double quotation marks; check only the text outside them. In all other fields, check the whole string.

On failure report the array, index, field, and about 40 characters of surrounding context so the offending sentence is findable.

## (b) No internal jargon leaking into customer text
Fail on, whole-word and case-insensitive, anywhere in any string INCLUDING inside quotes (these must never appear at all):
  - internal row IDs: `CAP-` followed by capitals/hyphens, `DRIFT-` followed by capitals/hyphens
  - pipeline vocabulary: req_id, REQ-<digits>, archetype, traceability, capability ledger, "the ledger"
  - implementation slang: fan-out, fans out, "fan out"
Report the matched term with its location.

Note: the bare word "ledger" may appear in a legitimate accounting sense in a customer document. Match "capability ledger" and "the ledger" specifically rather than every occurrence of "ledger".

## (c) Source citations must carry substantive context
Applies to `assumptions_made[].source` and to `conflicts[].source_a` / `source_b`.

The customer's complaint: a citation reading `discovery_call_01.txt — 'Priya and me.' [05:41]` is useless, because the reader cannot tell who "me" is or why that line supports the assumption.

Require every such citation to satisfy ALL of:
  1. names a real file that exists in `candidate/customer_packets/<packet>/`
  2. contains a quoted span (single or double quotes) of at least 15 characters
  3. that quoted span appears VERBATIM in the named file — normalize whitespace runs to a single space and normalize unicode quotes/apostrophes and dashes to ASCII before comparing, but do NOT lowercase. This extends quote-fidelity checking to the audit log itself, which is currently unchecked.
  4. carries attribution context beyond the bare quote: either a speaker name (a capitalized first and last name, e.g. `Priya Shetty`) or an explicit row/line locator (e.g. `row 12`, `line 47`). A bare timestamp like `[05:41]` is NOT sufficient on its own — that is precisely the case the customer rejected.

Report which of the four conditions failed, per citation.

## (d) Blocking flags ordered first
Within `missing_information_flags`, every entry with `blocking: true` must precede every entry with `blocking: false`, so the reader meets the blocking items first. Report the first out-of-order index.

content.text:
All four points are in, enforced by a check rather than by care. **68 style problems → 0**, all 8 checks green.

## What I measured before changing anything

Your two examples were symptoms: **36 pronoun usages** and **17 of 17** assumption citations with no attribution. A third leak you didn't flag — internal row IDs like `CAP-IT-ADMIN-SCOPE` were reaching customer text, because `proposed_manual_workaround` copied a ledger field written for internal readers.

## The two you flagged

Kevin O'Rourke's entry had four pronouns; it now names him throughout. And the citation:

> `discovery_call_01.txt` — **Diane Marsh (VP Finance, Acme Corp), [05:41], naming who should be able to administer the Ramp instance, change limits and add users:** *"Priya and me. And probably Sana in IT for the user-management side"*

Rather than write those by hand, citations are now **derived mechanically** — a helper finds the quote in the transcript, walks back to the nearest speaker marker, and returns speaker, role and timestamp. The attribution can't be wrong because it's read out of the file.

I also **extended that quote**: "Priya and me." is 13 characters, and the checker requires a 15-character verifiable span. A quote too short to verify is too short to cite.

## Point 3 — generalised, not patched

`check_audit_style.py` (182 lines) is now check 5 and gates every packet on five things: pronouns, jargon, citation quality, blocking-flags-first, dated evidence. Two design details worth knowing:

- **The pronoun rule exempts text inside quotation marks in a `source` field** — a customer is never misquoted to satisfy a style rule. The agent's test proved the span regex survives an apostrophe inside a quote (`anyone else's spend`), which a naive pattern would truncate.
- The ledger's 27 non-`SUPPORTED` rows gained a `customer_workaround` field. That's the leak fixed at the source rather than scrubbed per-packet.

## Point 4 — dual-write, as agreed

`deliverables/Acme_Corp/Acme_Corp_{Ramp_Config,Audit_Log}.json`, no trailing underscore. `out/` keeps the canonical names so Genera's tooling still finds them. **Packaging is blocked by a skipped check, not just a failing one** — a skip means the check didn't run, and these are the copies a customer receives.

## Two things I'd flag

I made **one deliberate relaxation**: a citation may name a project file (the shipped schema) instead of a customer document, since those are pointers, not quotations. I verified it didn't punch a hole — a fabricated filename and a fabricated quote both still fail.

And the **new-vendor approval remains the weakest entry**, unchanged by this pass. It's encoded as a zero-threshold tier that catches *all* software spend, not just new vendors. The audit log now says so plainly, but it's still a semantic mismatch rather than a faithful encoding — worth a line in NOTES.md.

**One recommendation I did not implement:** each `missing_information_flags` entry could name *who at Acme can answer it* (Marcus Webb for his own ceiling, Priya Shetty for the roster contradictions). Five blocking questions with no owner is a list; with owners it's a work assignment. Say the word and I'll add it before running packet C.

## Packet C — `client_c_apex_health`

### The controlling instrument

`security_requirements.doc` is a numbered vendor-response instrument, not a wish list. Its
own scope clause, lines 8–11:

> "These requirements apply to any corporate card or spend-management platform adopted by
> Apex Health Partners and are conditions of go-live. Requirements are numbered for
> reference in vendor responses. Each requirement must be answered as one of: ENFORCED BY
> PLATFORM / ENFORCED BY PROCESS / NOT MET."

And lines 56–58:

> "Responses must map each requirement to REQ number, state ENFORCED BY PLATFORM / ENFORCED
> BY PROCESS / NOT MET, and describe the mechanism. Vague responses ('the platform supports
> robust controls') will be returned."

**Practical effect on the audit log:** every C entry in `unsupported_api_requests` should
name its REQ number in `requested_feature` and state which of the three verdicts you are
claiming. That is the customer's own reporting format; use it.

The document is version 2.1, "approved by Risk Committee 2026-07-30". The call is
2026-08-06 — later, but it is corroboration, not amendment. **No stated doc-vs-call
precedence rule exists in this packet.** The document wins by its own scope clause; the
call adds detail and nowhere contradicts it.

`security_requirements.doc`, REQ-3, lines 31–39:

acceptance of one. So:

content.text:
Packet C done — **8/8 green**, both files validating. 35/35 quotes verified.

## The compliance document drove the shape

`security_requirements.doc` is a vendor-response instrument, not a wish list — it demands each requirement be answered `ENFORCED BY PLATFORM` / `ENFORCED BY PROCESS` / `NOT MET`, and warns that vague responses will be returned. The audit log answers all six in that format:

| | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **REQ-1** vendor prohibition | ENFORCED BY PLATFORM, with a standing process obligation |
| **REQ-2** activation gate | ENFORCED BY PROCESS — issue then suspend, release on confirmation |
| **REQ-3** pre-auth PO match | **NOT MET as written**; ENFORCED BY PROCESS via the fallback |
| **REQ-4** contract card expiry | ENFORCED BY PLATFORM (lock date) |
| **REQ-5** compliance read-only | ENFORCED BY PLATFORM (Auditor role) |
| **REQ-6** receipt capture | ENFORCED BY PLATFORM, configured in-app |

REQ-4 and REQ-5 are genuine wins, so they're answered in `assumptions_made` — filing a `SUPPORTED` capability as unsupported is precisely what the false-positive sweep exists to catch.

## The finding neither document states

**REQ-3 requires a purchase order above $500. The call sets the clinic per-transaction cap at $1,000.** So a $700 clinic purchase is approved by the card while sitting inside the PO requirement. Neither source notices; it only appears when you hold them side by side.

I encoded the $1,000 operational figure — $500 would block routine clinic buying — and raised it as **blocking**, since the compliance document is the controlling instrument and the gap falls inside its own threshold.

I also followed the precedence reference on reading the CFO note precisely: Compliance pre-authorizes **review** of a compensating control, not acceptance of one. REQ-3 is presented for review, not as agreed. That distinction is the difference between an honest answer and one that gets returned.

## A checker false positive, worth knowing about

The jargon rule matched `REQ-\d+`, meant to catch my pipeline's zero-padded internal ids (`REQ-001`) leaking into customer text. But Apex numbers its requirements `REQ-1`…`REQ-6` and *requires* responses to cite them — so my checker was rejecting the customer's own mandated vocabulary. Narrowed to `REQ-\d{3,}`. Packet A re-verified green after the change.

A rule that was right for packet A was wrong for packet C. That's the argument for running more than one packet before trusting a gate.

## Caveat on this config

**This packet has no roster and no email address anywhere** — not one. Six people are named; the fourteen clinic managers, the central finance team and the contract nurses are all unnamed. Email addresses use an invented `apexhealth.example` domain, flagged blocking with the invention stated explicitly. Eight blocking flags in total, and the three-week go-live for clinic managers cannot be met until those names arrive.

Packet D next — the messy one, where the two sources actively disagree and the headline conflict should stay blocking rather than resolve by recency.

The most important gap: **the pipeline demands rich citations but ships no tool to produce them.** I hand-wrote a throwaway citation helper for packet A, then wrote a *second* one for packet C. Transcript with speakers:
```
discovery_call_01.txt — Diane Marsh (VP Finance, Acme Corp), [05:41], <context>: "<verbatim quote>"
```
Structured/line-addressed file:
```

security_requirements.doc, line 16 — <context>: "<verbatim quote>"
```
The `<context>` is a human-written clause the caller supplies. Everything else you derive from the file.

# CLI

```
python3 cite.py --packet <packet_name> --quote "<verbatim text>" [--context "<clause>"] [--repo <path>]
python3 cite.py --packet <packet_name> --speakers        # show the speaker map you detected
```

- `--quote`: locate this text across every file in the packet and emit the citation. Match after the same whitespace/unicode folding `check_audit_style.py` uses, so a quote typed with ASCII punctuation still finds curly-quoted source. Print the citation to stdout.

6. `*.csv` — cite by row number, where row 1 is the header. Emit the whole row as the quote.

1. Packet A: quote `I never want to see a decline` → must attribute to Diane Marsh with role and timestamp.
2. Packet A: quote `Priya and me. And probably Sana in IT for the user-management side` → Diane Marsh, [05:41].
3. Packet A CSV: quote `Jenny Park` → must produce a `row 15` citation with the full row.

9. `--speakers` on packets A, C and D.
10. **Round-trip proof (the important one):** take the citations your script generates, drop them into a copy of a real audit_log.json under /tmp, and run `check_audit_style.py --repo` against it. Clean up anything created outside the repo.

In your final message report: the final line count, the exact citation string produced for tests 1-7, and the result of test 10.

58	the grading rubric. Adopt its numbering and its vocabulary verbatim in the audit log.

content.text:
Packet C was the first packet with a different *shape* rather than different content, so its lessons are mostly about robustness. Everything below is implemented, pushed, and both packets re-verify 8/8.

## The gap that mattered most

**The pipeline demanded attributed citations and shipped no tool to produce them.** I hand-wrote a throwaway helper for packet A, then a second for packet C. A fresh session would write a third — and hand-written attribution is exactly where citations go wrong.

`cite.py` is the permanent version. It derives speaker, role and timestamp *from the file* and handles every format in the set:

| Format | Output |
|---|---|
| Attendee-block transcript (A, C) | `Diane Marsh (VP Finance, Acme Corp), [01:14]` |
| Slack export (D) | `Leo Novak (CEO), [2026-07-30 08:55]` |
| Numbered requirements doc (C) | `line 16 — document owner M. Vance (Director of Compliance)` |
| Spanish policy memo (B) | `section 5.3 (line 71)` |
| Markdown notes (D) | `line 19` fallback |
| CSV (A) | `row 15` with the full row |

I checked it invents nothing — the Slack role and the memo's owner are both parsed from real header lines (`Members: leo.novak (CEO)…`, `Preparada por: Joaquín Esparza…`). And the property that matters: **its output passes the citation gate**, proven on packet D's Slack format, which the pipeline has never run.

## Making the packet C finding repeatable

The $500-vs-$1,000 straddle was caught by hand. On an unseen packet it would likely be missed, so `money_map.py` collates every monetary figure by amount:

```
   500.00 USD   discovery_call_apex.txt:36,54,78, security_requirements.doc:32
 1,000.00 USD   discovery_call_apex.txt:20, 22
```

The REQ-3 threshold and the spelled-out "a per-transaction cap of a thousand" land adjacent — that's the signature. It **asserts nothing**; adjacency is a prompt to look, not a claim. A tool that guessed at conflicts would put false ones in an audit log, which is worse than missing one.

## Four rules that can't be scripted

1. **Read the packet on its own terms before extracting.** Does a document dictate how it must be answered? Who exists, and can they be identified? What's absent entirely? I reordered Phase 1 so this comes first, because it does.
2. **The customer's vocabulary outranks house style.** My jargon check rejected `REQ-1` as internal — it was Apex's own mandated numbering. If a check fires on something the customer requires, fix the check, don't launder their language.
3. **Where a fully-supported requirement goes** when every numbered item needs an answer: `assumptions_made` with the verdict first. Never `unsupported_api_requests` — the false-positive sweep would correctly reject it.
4. **The identity convention when there's no roster at all**, which is packet C: named people with flagged placeholders beat an empty `users` array.

Plus two idioms now recurring across both packets: a group limit must state its cardinality in `notes`, and a non-amount-shaped rule still encodes as a zero-threshold tier that over-captures and must be logged as such.

## One thing I'd flag

`cite.py` is 238 lines against a ~40-line project guardrail. I think it earns the exception — 15 functions, longest is 28 lines, and it replaces per-packet rework — but it's the one place the "small scripts" constraint bent, and worth a sentence in NOTES.md rather than hoping nobody notices.

Packet D next is the real test of all this: no clean documents, two sources that actively disagree, and a headline conflict that must stay blocking rather than resolve by recency.

The spelled-out form collates correctly — `raw:"a thousand"` → `amount_cents:100000`, identical to `raw:"$1,000"`. A second bonus adjacency shows up: `10,000` from REQ-2 and from the call.

## Tests 2–7
- **A (44 figures):** `$500`, `five hundred (dollars)`, `five thousand` + `five-thousand` (the hyphenated "over-five-thousand tier"), `Fifty grand`→$50,000, `two thousand`, `eight thousand`, `ten thousand`, `seventy-five dollars`→$75, `A ten-dollar`→$10, plus all 30 roster `Target_Limit_USD_Monthly` cells (period `monthly` read off the header). **"cap it at ten to be safe" is NOT detected** — a bare unit word with no scale and no currency is indistinguishable from "ten clinics", and reporting it would open the floodgates. It is visible in the context line printed for the $8,000 figure on the same line 41 ("Call it eight thousand a month, cap it at ten to be safe"), which is the best I can do honestly.
- **B (29 figures):** MXN and BRL captured and marked non-USD with `*` in both sections; amounts are grouped by currency and never converted. `$1,500 MXN`, `R$ 450`, `R$ 6.000`→6,000.00 (dot read as a thousands separator), `USD $1,200`. - **D (16 figures):** `$60k`, `$30k/mo`, `$18k/yr`, `$10k/mo`, bare `1k`→$1,000 all handled. **A range is reported as its two endpoints, each tagged `range`**, sharing one context line: `$50-60k` → 50,000.00 and 60,000.00 (the `k` is applied to both endpoints — ranges are matched before the plain numeric detector precisely so `$50-60k` isn't read as $50 and $60,000). `$60k` from the notes then collates with `$60k` from Slack.
- **E (13 figures):** `Monthly_Cap_USD` and `Per_Transaction_Cap_USD` read as money from the header; `Headcount`, `Allowed_MCCs`/`Blocked_MCCs` correctly ignored (no MCC code, no headcount appears as a figure). Header drives period (`monthly`) and scope (`per_transaction`).
- **No years, dates, times, version numbers or phone-like digits** in any of the five: bare digits are reported only from a header-declared money column, and everything else needs a `$`/`R$`, a currency word, or a `k`. Verified the full distinct-`raw` set for all five packets.
- **`--json` parses** for all five (`{"packet", "figures":[{file,line,raw,amount_cents,currency,period,scope,context}]}`); exit 0 in every case including a bad `--packet`, no `--packet`, and running from `/tmp` (paths resolve from `__file__`, `--repo` honored).

## Known limits (please keep these in the write-up rather than assume coverage)
1. Bare unit words with no scale and no currency word ("cap it at ten") are not detected — deliberate precision tradeoff.
2. Spanish/Portuguese hundreds words beyond `quinientos`/`quinhentos` (e.g. `doscientos`) are not in the table; they were absent as money in packet B, and adding them raises headcount-noise risk.
3. `period` is read from a ±25–32 character window around the figure, so a line stating two things ("four thousand a month … cap of a thousand") tags the nearer figure correctly but can leave the other's period blank rather than wrong; `scope` is line-wide by design, so tags can be over-inclusive on dense lines.
4. Currency is inferred from the nearest marker; a spelled-out amount with no marker anywhere on its line defaults to USD. Every non-USD figure is marked `*`, but an unmarked figure is an inference, not a statement from the source.
5. Ranges become two endpoints — the tool does not represent "between X and Y" as a single object.
6. Repeated identical amounts on one line are reported once per occurrence (e.g. "over a thousand" twice on packet C line 20); that is intentional, since each occurrence carries different surrounding text.</result>

content.text:
For a **fresh Claude Code session**, one instruction:

```
Run the ramp-deployment skill on client_d_hypergrowth
```

That loads `SKILL.md` and the session drives the rest. The skill's description auto-triggers on this phrasing, so you don't need the slash form — though `/ramp-deployment client_d_hypergrowth` works too.

Under it, there are **two** shell commands, not one, and that's deliberate:

```bash
python3 run_pipeline.py --packet client_d_hypergrowth            # Phase 0: setup + runbook
#   ... session does Phases 1-3, guided by SKILL.md ...
python3 run_pipeline.py --packet client_d_hypergrowth --verify   # Phase 4: 8 checks + package
```

The gap between them is the judgment work — reading the transcripts, resolving conflicts, deciding what Ramp genuinely can't do. That can't be a subprocess, which is why Phase 0's runbook ends by naming the `--verify` command as the next step: a session that follows the printed output top to bottom lands in the right place without needing to be told.

The exercise README explicitly allows "the equivalent instruction to a fresh Claude Code / Codex session," so the natural-language form is the intended single command. `--verify` on a green run also writes the customer-named copies to `deliverables/`.

If you want to see the packet list first: `python3 run_pipeline.py --list`.

content.text:
Packet D done — **8/8 green**. All three core packets (A, C, D) are complete.

## The headline conflict stayed blocking

The February notes record Leo agreeing to a $2,500 tiered threshold for Q2. A later Slack message from the same person demands all travel route to him. Recency *and* authority both favour the later message, and I encoded it — but resolving on recency alone would have been wrong here, because four things point the other way:

- the earlier source documents an agreement **Leo himself made**
- Maya states plainly she wasn't in the meeting and can't find confirmation or cancellation
- the June revisit was **cancelled and never rescheduled**
- Dev asked in the channel whether the two were compatible and **got no reply**

Both arrangements are emitted side by side in `approval_policies`, the second labelled as not active, so a reviewer sees the choice rather than inheriting mine. Flagged blocking: this needs an answer from Leo, not an inference.

## A conflict the packet doesn't state

Stan is to own the software card personally *and* be unable to touch limits. Those can't both hold — the Ramp role granting user administration without spend authority also prevents holding a card or seeing spend. I encoded the restriction (stated by the Head of Finance about someone else's access) over the ownership claim (that person describing his own preference), left the software card unassigned, and raised it blocking.

## The new tooling paid off on first contact

`money_map` immediately surfaced that **$2,500 appears in both files meaning two different things** — the February travel threshold and the GTM IC limit. jj had asked whether they were the same and been told separate, so both are encoded distinctly with the collision risk recorded. I would not reliably have caught that by reading.

## Two checker findings, both correct, both mine

The **false-positive sweep** caught REQ-013/REQ-014 pointing at an unsupported entry while mapped to a `SUPPORTED` archetype — a real mis-mapping I'd have shipped.

More interesting: **two citations failed the 15-character span rule because the source text itself contains embedded double quotes**, which breaks span detection. `cite.py` produced them and `check_audit_style.py` rejected them — the tool and its gate disagreeing. I re-cited against spans without inner quotes, but that's a genuine `cite.py` limitation worth noting rather than a one-off.

Also explicitly *not* built on: the NetSuite message, retracted by its author in the same breath, recorded as a deliberate omission. Contractors excluded from users entirely, as instructed.

**Next is NOTES.md** — the last required deliverable, and the one the spec says never to cut. I have five verification-delta cases banked, well past the two required. B and E remain optional.
