content.text:
Both fixed, all three packets re-verified **9/9 green**. Re-rendered viewer above.

## 1. Emails → `N/A`

You're right, and the reason it's worse than an empty field is the point: `leo.novak@hypergrowth.example` is indistinguishable from a real address to whoever runs the deployment. Invite it and you either get a silent failure or you mail a stranger. An empty field at least announces itself.

Fixed in C and D (packet A was fine — its roster has real addresses). Cardholders are now identified by name in each limit's `display_name`, so an `N/A` address doesn't make the limit ambiguous.

**Enforced mechanically** as new check 8: every email domain must appear somewhere in the customer's own documents, or the value must be `N/A`. Packet A passes with 90 real addresses; C and D failed until fixed. A missing *name* may still be `"(surname pending roster)"` — a name is descriptive, an address is actionable.

## 2. Cloud computing — I got this wrong twice

**The rationale was thin.** I reasoned that 340 vendor subscriptions at 82 employees probably includes infrastructure. The packet never mentions cloud, AWS, or infrastructure. That's inference, not evidence.

**The flagging was worse, and it's the part your question exposes.** The only trace was a line in the config's `translation_notes` saying "confirm, since it was not named explicitly." That is **not a flag** — there was no `assumptions_made` entry and no `missing_information_flags` question. The audit log is what the customer reads, and it said nothing. So the honest answer to "how is this flag evident to the customer?" is: it wasn't.

I withdrew it rather than better-documenting it. The programme now permits `SaaS / Software` only, with an assumption stating plainly that infrastructure will decline and that the wider mapping was dropped, plus a question asking whether cloud should be in scope before the first billing cycle.

The general rule, now in SKILL.md: **never widen a permission by inference.** Narrowing is recoverable — a decline gets reported and fixed. Widening grants spend nobody authorised and surfaces nothing. And an inference that changes what a card accepts belongs in the audit log, not a config note.

Worth noting my own false-negative sweep couldn't have caught this — it only fires on `UNSUPPORTED`/`UI_ONLY`/`PARTIAL` archetypes, and category restriction is `SUPPORTED`. The gap was silently *widening* a supported capability, which no check was looking for. That's now a documented rule rather than a check, because "is this inference too generous?" is judgement, not something I can test mechanically.

content.text:
Yes — three findings, and one of them is worse than the Cloud computing case.

## Both CEOs held admin rights nobody granted

**Acme:** Diane answered "who should administer the instance?" with *"Priya and me. And probably Sana in IT for the user-management side."* Marcus wasn't in that list. I gave him `BUSINESS_ADMIN` anyway, inferring it from "CEO".

**Hypergrowth is worse.** Rachel said *"me and maya as admins"* — and then, asked why Maya rather than Leo, said: *"because leo will ask you to change things and i'd rather you do it than him. he clicks fast and reads slow."* That's the packet explicitly stating the CEO should not be making account changes. **I granted him admin anyway.** Not silence I filled in — evidence I overrode.

Both are now Business Users. Approving travel needs no admin rights, so nothing either CEO was asked to do is blocked. All three packets now grant administration to exactly the named people:

| Acme Corp | Diane Marsh, Priya Shetty |
|---|---|
| **Apex Health** | Gordon Pryce, Dana Whitfield |
| **Hypergrowth** | Rachel Kim, Maya Osei |

## Apex had reimbursements enabled on three of four programmes

The words "reimbursement" and "expense claim" appear **nowhere** in that packet. Pure inference — I'd carried the pattern over from packet A, where it *was* stated. All four are now card-only, with the likeliest real exception (nurse mileage, which was named) raised as a question rather than assumed. Same fix on Hypergrowth's offsite programme.

## Root cause was my own ledger

`DRIFT-ROLE-BUSINESS-OWNER` said to map an owner to `BUSINESS_ADMIN`, following the Westbrook sample. But Westbrook's Priti *runs that company's finances* — the sample's mapping was right for Priti and wrong to generalise. The row now says to map by the administrative responsibility a packet actually assigns, never by job title. That's the fix that stops it recurring on the sixth packet.

## One thing I deliberately did not change

Apex's clinic programme keeps **General merchandise** as the nearest category to "hardware stores." Hardware *was* explicitly requested, so this is a documented lossy translation of a stated need — different from Cloud computing, which was never mentioned at all. It stays flagged in both an assumption and an open question. Worth knowing I considered and rejected narrowing it, in case you'd call that differently.

All three re-verify **9/9 green**, viewers re-rendered. NOTES.md is the remaining deliverable.

content.text:
That traced further than I expected. Nothing changed — here's what the sample actually did to the build.

## Idioms that carried through and generalised well

Every one of these appears in all three outputs, and most became explicit rules rather than copied shapes:

| Sample idiom | What it became |
|---|---|
| `approval_policies[].source` holding a verbatim quote | seeded the whole citation-quality standard, and eventually `cite.py` |
| `$50` receipt rule in `assumptions_made`, absent from config | the **omit-and-flag** rule, now the routing table for `UI_ONLY` verdicts |
| Evidence as *"docs.ramp.com, checked 2026-08-24 — no notifications resource; nearest primitive is `POST /webhooks`"* | the ledger's `evidence_line` contract, copied verbatim into every audit log |
| Workaround naming a **route to the outcome**, not just a refusal | the ledger's `workaround` / `customer_workaround` fields |
| `"(surname pending roster)"` + blocking flag | the identity convention |
| Group limit stating fan-out in `notes` | mandatory cardinality rule (A:1, C:3, D:6 limits) |
| `{threshold: 0, approver: "AUTO"}` as an explicit tier | every policy across all three packets |
| `conflicts: []` being legitimate | *"an empty array is a claim you are making, not a default"* |

## Two places the sample was wrong or narrow, and I caught it

**Category spelling.** The sample writes `"Software / SaaS"`; the API's canonical name is `"SaaS / Software"`. It validates either way — free strings — so this is a silent error in the shipped example. I used the API spelling and recorded the discrepancy in the ledger.

**`conflicts: []`** is right for Westbrook (one email, one author) but is the single most anchoring thing in the sample. My packets run 5 / 3 / 5.

## Two places I over-generalised from it — one you already caught

**The N/A bug traces directly here.** Westbrook shows a placeholder for a missing *name*. I extended that to a missing *address*, which is exactly where the pattern breaks: a name is descriptive, an address is actionable. The sample never faces this, because both its users have real email domains from the intake email.

**Owner → `BUSINESS_ADMIN`** — corrected an hour ago. Westbrook's Priti runs that company's finances; Acme's Marcus and Hypergrowth's Leo were both explicitly excluded from their admin lists.

## The one that stings

The sample sets `reimbursements_enabled: false`, and its intake email **never mentions reimbursements**. So it already demonstrated the conservative default: *not mentioned → off*. I enabled reimbursements on three Apex programmes anyway, in a packet that likewise never mentions them. That wasn't a gap in the sample — it was me not following an example that was right there.

## What the sample simply cannot teach

2 users, 2 departments, 1 programme, 2 limits — all hand-writable. It has nothing to say about group fan-out at scale, onboarding 82 people with no roster, populations known only as headcounts, or a packet that dictates its own response format. Those conventions came from the packets themselves, which is why C and D forced more skill changes than A did.

content.text:
Yes, there's a rule — and checking it surfaced a real inconsistency.

## The rule as it stands

| Situation | Emit | Flag |
|---|---|---|
| Email/domain absent | literal `N/A` — never a constructed address | blocking |
| Name part missing | `"(surname pending roster)"` | blocking |
| Headcount but no names | group limit with count + basis in `notes` | blocking |
| Population varies | plan on the upper figure, say so | blocking |

The stated reason for the asymmetry: **a name is descriptive, an address is actionable.** A reader seeing `Bruno (surname pending roster)` understands the gap and moves on. A reader seeing `bruno.walsh@apexhealth.example` may well invite it.

## Two problems I found

**1. The wording is wrong for packet C.** Bruno is recorded as `"(surname pending roster)"` — but Apex Health has **no roster**, pending or otherwise. Nobody in that packet ever mentions one. The phrase was inherited from Westbrook, where a roster genuinely *was* coming, and from packet D, where the PEO export genuinely *is* pending. For Apex it asserts a document that doesn't exist.

The placeholder should say why the name is missing in *that* packet's terms — something like `"(surname not stated)"` — rather than borrowing Westbrook's reason.

**2. The name rule is instruction-only.** The email rule has check 8 behind it; no script looks at `first_name` or `last_name` at all. So a fresh session could write `last_name: "Unknown"`, `"TBD"`, `""`, or invent a plausible surname, and nothing would catch it. Given that inventing a *surname* is nearly as bad as inventing an address — it produces a person who doesn't exist — that's a thinner guard than the topic deserves.

## What I'd propose

Two small changes, both narrow:

- **Generalise the placeholder to state its own reason**: `"(surname pending roster)"` where a roster is genuinely coming, `"(surname not stated)"` where the packet simply never gives one. Fix Bruno accordingly.
- **Add a check** that any parenthesised placeholder in a name field matches an approved form and is paired with a blocking flag — closing the gap where `"TBD"` or a fabricated surname would pass silently.

I haven't changed anything. Say the word and I'll do both, or just the Bruno wording if you'd rather not add a tenth check.

content.text:
Both done, all three packets **9/9 green**.

## 1. The placeholder now states its own reason

Two approved forms, and choosing between them is a factual claim about the packet:

- `"(surname pending roster)"` — where a roster genuinely *is* coming (Westbrook, Hypergrowth's PEO export)
- `"(surname not stated)"` — where the packet simply never gives one

Bruno is now `(surname not stated)`, since Apex has no roster and never mentions one. Small thing, but the old wording asserted a document that doesn't exist.

## 2. Check 8 now covers names as well as addresses

Folded into the existing check rather than a tenth row — it's one concern, fabricated identity. It enforces the form, rejects `TBD` / `Unknown` / `N/A` / empty in a name field, and requires a blocking flag that names the person.

Verified by mutation against real packet C output:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `(TBD)` | caught — not an approved placeholder |
| `Unknown` | caught — reads as a blank, not a declaration |
| `N/A` in a name field | caught — reserved for addresses |
| placeholder, flag doesn't name Bruno | caught — no blocking flag mentions `'Bruno'` |
| **invented surname `Walsh`** | **not caught** — control |

That last row is the honest limit. There's no domain to check a name against, so a plausible fabricated surname passes. The rule leans on *declaration form* precisely because it can't detect fabrication — which is worth knowing rather than assuming check 8 makes names safe.

## One correction to something I said mid-task

My first test run reported all four cases as **MISSED**, and I nearly acted on that. The check was working fine — my filter looked for a separate detail block, which single-line failures don't produce; the failure appears inline in the results table. The test was wrong, not the code. I re-ran against raw output before concluding anything.

Remaining: **NOTES.md**, the last required deliverable. B and E stay optional.

1	LLAMADA DE DESCUBRIMIENTO — LOGÍSTICA GLOBEX, S.A. DE C.V.
     2	Fecha: 2026-08-04 · Duración: 38 min
     3	Participantes:
     4	  - Alejandra Vidal, Directora de Finanzas (CFO), Logística Globex (AV)
     5	  - Rubén Ortega, Director de Operaciones, Logística Globex (RO)
     6	  - Camila Duarte, Deployment Lead, Genera (en representación de Ramp) (CD)
     7	Transcripción automática; el audio original está en español. Marcas de tiempo aproximadas.
     8	
     9	[00:00] CD: Ya estamos grabando. Alejandra, Rubén, gracias por el tiempo. El objetivo de hoy es entender cómo manejan los gastos para configurar su instancia de Ramp. Yo pregunto, ustedes me corrigen.
    10	
    11	[00:16] AV: Perfecto. Te doy el contexto primero. Somos una empresa de logística con sede en Monterrey. Unos doscientos empleados en México, de los cuales más o menos sesenta necesitan capacidad de gasto. Y este trimestre estamos abriendo dos oficinas nuevas: São Paulo y Miami.
    12	
    13	[00:38] CD: ¿Las dos oficinas nuevas ya existen legalmente?
    14	
    15	[00:42] AV: Miami sí — Globex Logistics USA LLC, ya está constituida, ya tiene cuenta bancaria. São Paulo está en proceso. Los abogados dicen que la entidad brasileña — va a ser Globex Logística do Brasil Ltda. — estará lista a fin de septiembre. Pero no queremos esperar a septiembre para diseñar todo; queremos que el día que exista la entidad, todo esté listo para prender el switch.
    16	
    17	[01:07] CD: Entendido. Entonces diseñamos las tres estructuras ahora, y lo de Brasil queda pendiente de la entidad legal. ¿Cómo se organiza la operación en México?
    18	
    19	[01:18] RO: Tres áreas grandes. Operaciones — choferes, supervisores de patio, coordinadores de ruta. Es el grueso, unas cuarenta personas con gasto. Luego Administración — finanzas, recursos humanos, sistemas. Y Comercial — ventas y atención a clientes, unas doce personas.
    20	
    21	[01:39] CD: ¿Y el gasto de Operaciones es principalmente qué?
    22	
    23	[01:43] RO: Combustible, casetas, viáticos. Cada chofer carga diésel dos o tres veces por semana. Hoy funciona con vales físicos y es un desastre administrativo. Queremos tarjeta por chofer, restringida a gasolineras — que no sirva en otra cosa, ni OXXO ni nada — con límite diario. Mil quinientos pesos por día por chofer.
    24	
    25	[02:08] CD: Mil quinientos pesos mexicanos, límite diario, solo gasolineras. ¿Los supervisores?
    26	
    27	[02:15] RO: Los supervisores tres mil pesos al día, y además de combustible pueden pagar refacciones menores y casetas. Los coordinadores de ruta no necesitan tarjeta; ellos no gastan.
    28	
    29	[02:27] AV: Y ojo — Camila, esto es importante — todo el gasto de México se maneja en pesos. No quiero que mis gerentes en Monterrey estén pensando en dólares. Los límites, los reportes, todo en moneda local. En Brasil igual: reales. En Miami, dólares.
    30	
    31	[02:46] CD: Cada país en su moneda local. ¿Y para consolidar?
    32	
    33	[02:50] AV: Para consolidar, mi equipo y yo vemos todo en dólares. La política que les mandé — el memo — tiene los topes por categoría, algunos están en pesos, otros en reales, otros en dólares, según quién lo escribió. Sé que es un revoltijo. Confío en que ustedes lo normalicen y me digan qué asumieron.
    34	
    35	[03:09] CD: Lo normalizamos y documentamos el tipo de cambio que usemos. ¿Comercial y Administración?
    36	
    37	[03:16] RO: Comercial viaja mucho — visitan clientes en todo el norte del país, y ahora van a empezar a viajar a Brasil y Estados Unidos. Tarjeta física para todos los de Comercial, límite mensual de veinte mil pesos, categorías de viaje: vuelos, hoteles, restaurantes, transporte. Administración casi no gasta; tarjeta virtual con límite bajo, cinco mil pesos al mes, para suscripciones y cosas de oficina.
    38	
    39	[03:45] AV: Las suscripciones de software las quiero centralizadas, igual que les comenté que hacía mi colega de otra empresa — una sola tarjeta virtual para todo el software, la maneja sistemas, y cualquier proveedor nuevo pasa por mí.
    40	
    41	[03:59] CD: Muy bien — programa de software centralizado, lo mismo que hacemos con otros clientes. ¿Monto?
    42	
    43	[04:04] AV: Ponle veinticinco mil pesos mensuales.
    44	
    45	[04:08] CD: ¿Aprobaciones en general?
    46	
    47	[04:11] AV: Sencillo. Hasta dos mil pesos, automático. De dos mil a veinte mil, aprueba el jefe directo. Arriba de veinte mil, apruebo yo. Y en Brasil y Miami la misma lógica cuando arranquen, con los montos equivalentes — no idénticos, equivalentes. Redondeados a números que tengan sentido localmente.
    48	
    49	[04:33] CD: ¿Quién administra la instancia?
    50	
    51	[04:37] AV: Yo y Joaquín, mi gerente de contabilidad. Y en cada país va a haber un administrador local cuando arranquen — en Miami ya sabemos que es Elena Ruiz, la gerente de oficina. En São Paulo todavía no contratamos al equipo administrativo. Hay tres choferes brasileños ya contratados, empiezan en octubre, y el gerente de operaciones de allá, Thiago Moreira, ya firmó — él sí ya existe, ya tiene correo de la empresa.
    52	
    53	[05:04] CD: ¿Los empleados de Brasil los damos de alta ahora o cuando exista la entidad?
    54	
    55	[05:09] AV: Diseñen todo ahora. Si el sistema permite dejarlos listos sin activar, mejor. Si no, díganme qué se puede y qué no — no me inventen. Prefiero una lista de "esto queda manual" a una sorpresa en octubre.
    56	
    57	[05:22] CD: Así lo hacemos. ¿Algo más que deba saber?
    58	
    59	[05:26] RO: Los viáticos de los choferes — hoteles de carretera, comidas — hoy se manejan con efectivo y reembolsos. Quisiéramos meterlos a la tarjeta también, pero la realidad es que muchos hoteles de carretera en México solo aceptan efectivo. Así que los reembolsos no se pueden matar del todo, aunque el memo diga que sí.
    60	
    61	[05:45] AV: El memo es aspiracional en esa parte. [ríe] Hazle caso a Rubén.
    62	
    63	[05:49] CD: Entendido — el memo dice una cosa, la operación dice otra; gana la operación y lo dejo anotado. Última: ¿fecha objetivo?
    64	
    65	[05:57] AV: México en cuatro semanas. Miami cuando esté el equipo, digamos seis semanas. Brasil, cuando exista la entidad. Y Camila — el resumen ejecutivo que me mandes, en español por favor. Mi consejo lo lee en español.
    66	
    67	[06:09] CD: Hecho. Gracias a los dos.
    68	
    69	[FIN DE LA TRANSCRIPCIÓN]

content.text:
Packet B done — **9/9 green**. Four of five packets complete. 43/43 quotes verified, including the accented Spanish and Portuguese.

## The currency question resolved cleanly

**Limits were not converted at all** — 5 in MXN, 3 in BRL, 2 in USD — because Ramp carries a currency per limit and Alejandra was explicit: *"Los límites, los reportes, todo en moneda local."* That requirement is met directly.

Only the **approval thresholds** needed a rate, and only because this configuration format has a single `threshold_usd_cents` field while Globex sets thresholds in three currencies. That's a limitation of the exercise schema, not of Ramp — worth saying plainly so nobody concludes Ramp can't do multi-currency approvals.

Converted at 18.0 MXN and 5.5 BRL, each policy's `source` line preserving the original local figures, rate flagged **blocking**. Memo §5.2 pre-authorises exactly this — *"utilizar un tipo de cambio razonable y documentarlo"* — the same shape as packet C's compensating control: a customer granting the fallback in writing. I was explicit that no live rate source was available.

## Three conflicts

**Reimbursements** resolve rather than stay open — two independent signals agree: Ortega's dissent written *inside the memo itself*, and the CFO on the call (*"El memo es aspiracional en esa parte. Hazle caso a Rubén."*).

**The second came from reading, not tooling.** The call describes the Administración card as covering *"suscripciones y cosas de oficina"*, while the memo assigns **all** software to one central card with every new vendor pre-approved by Finance. Those statements are nine lines apart on the same call. Encoded as office expenses only, raised as a question.

**The third is a negative finding.** The memo declares itself unharmonised and carries the language-precedence rule (Spanish wins, except §4 whose original is English) — but no discrepancy needed it, because §2, §3 and §4 each govern a different entity and never state the same figure twice. Logged so the absence reads as *checked* rather than assumed.

## Two things worth your attention

**Nothing in this config binds a person to a legal entity.** The format's `locations` carry only a name and a country — no entity field. Three entities are recorded, each person has a location, but the link is made in Ramp during setup. That's the sharpest schema-expressiveness gap any packet has hit.

**The Spanish executive summary is a delivery obligation these files can't satisfy.** Alejandra asked for it because her board reads Spanish. It's recorded in the audit log so it isn't lost, but it's a separate document — say the word and I'll draft it.

My own checks caught two things before shipping: a `UI_ONLY` entity requirement configured with no audit trace, and eight pronouns in text I'd just written.

Only packet E remains, then NOTES.md.

    12	
    13	[00:24] CD: And the spend problem?
    14	
    15	[00:27] CJ: Field reps buy things constantly — gas, parking, materials from hardware stores, occasionally a hotel if a job runs long.     16	
    17	[00:47] AN: The key word is role-based. We have six field roles and each one should only be able to buy what their job needs. I built a matrix — you have it, the CSV — mapping each role to allowed and blocked merchant category codes. I pulled the MCC codes from our old amex reporting, so those are real codes from actual historical transactions.
    18	
    19	[01:06] CD: I have the matrix. Walk me through the philosophy — allow-first or block-first?
    20	
    21	[01:11] AN: Allow-first. Default deny. A merchandising rep has no business at an electronics store, and an installer has no business booking flights. The matrix's ALLOWED column is the whole universe of what that role can buy; the BLOCKED column is me being extra explicit about categories we've had incidents with — belt and suspenders.
    22	
    23	[01:31] CD: Understood. I'll map your matrix onto the control primitives the platform actually has — allow-lists and block-lists work a bit differently there — and I'll show you exactly how each rule translates, including anywhere the translation isn't one-to-one.
    24	
    25	[01:44] AN: That's what I want to see. If some rule can't be enforced exactly as written I need to know which one and what the closest enforceable version is.
    26	
    27	[01:52] CD: Limits per role?
    28	
    29	[01:55] CJ: In the matrix — last two columns. Monthly cap and per-transaction cap per role. District managers are higher, seasonal reps are lowest.
    30	
    31	[02:03] CD: And the seasonal piece — tell me about that.
    32	
    33	[02:07] CJ: That's the part I care most about.     34	
    35	[02:33] CD: Auto-expiry on a fixed date is natively supported — we set an end date on each seasonal card and it locks itself that day. Extension is a one-field change if you keep someone into January.
    36	
    37	[02:42] CJ: Perfect. Some do convert to permanent, maybe one in ten.
    38	
    39	[02:46] CD: Virtual or physical cards for the field?
    40	
    41	[02:49] CJ: Virtual, in the phone wallet — that's how the reps live. Physical only for district managers.
    42	
    43	[02:55] AN: One operational thing: we onboard seasonal reps in weekly waves — thirty to forty per week for four weeks. Whatever the setup process is, it can't require me clicking through a UI form one hundred forty times. I have the reps in a spreadsheet: name, email, role, district, start date, end date. I want to hand the system the spreadsheet.
    44	
    45	[03:12] CD: Bulk creation from your data is exactly what we'll spec — that's an API-driven flow. I'll flag anything about it that isn't fully automatable.
    46	
    47	[03:19] AN: Good. Approvals?
    48	
    49	[03:21] CJ: For the field, none — the card rules ARE the policy. That's the whole point of doing role-based controls. If the card allows it, it's approved. District managers review a weekly exceptions report instead of approving in advance.
    50	
    51	[03:33] AN: HQ is different — normal manager approvals over five hundred dollars — but HQ is twenty people and boring. The field is the product here.
    52	
    53	[03:40] CD: Who administers?
    54

    56

    58	
    59	[03:57] CJ: The permanent field force migrates in September. Seasonal wave one is October 19th — that date does not move.
    60	
    61	[04:03] CD: Understood. Config draft to you both this week.
    62	
    63	[END OF TRANSCRIPT]

content.text:
**All five packets complete**, each 9/9 green. 180 requirements extracted, every quote verified against source, 193 audit entries, 28 blocking.

| Packet | Reqs | Assum | Missing | Conflicts | Unsupported |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Acme | 37 | 17 | 10 (5 blocking) | 5 | 11 |
| Logística Globex | 43 | 14 | 10 (5) | 3 | 11 |
| Apex Health | 35 | 13 | 13 (8) | 3 | 11 |
| Hypergrowth | 37 | 15 | 14 (7) | 5 | 7 |
| Vanguard | 28 | 12 | 8 (3) | 1 | 10 |

## The translation splits in two directions

This is the packet `CATEGORY_MAP` was built for, and the honest answer to Ahmed's question — *"if some rule can't be enforced exactly as written I need to know which one"* — has two halves:

- **The BLOCKED column survives exactly.** Ramp can block specific MCCs, so all six blocked lists are recorded verbatim.
- **The ALLOWED column never does.** Ramp allow-lists on its own categories, so twelve codes across six roles collapse to ten. Six imprecise mappings, named individually rather than summarised — the widest being `5200`/`5251` (hardware, home supply) widening to General merchandise.

The default-deny *philosophy* is preserved exactly, though. Anything outside a role's categories is refused. It's the granularity that's lost, not the posture.

## The finding neither document contains

The seasonal and trainer rows allow `5541` but **not** `5542` — attended service stations but not automated pumps. Both are Ramp's Fuel and gas category, so permitting one permits the other. **Seasonal reps gain unattended-pump access the matrix deliberately excludes.**

Raised blocking, because whether that exclusion was intentional decides whether this is a gap to manage or a typo in the matrix — and the answer costs nothing to get.

## Where an earlier correction paid off

District manager visibility is **answered rather than refused**. Ramp scopes visibility to a manager's reporting line, so setting each rep's manager to their DM delivers it without a custom role. Had I not corrected `CAP-SCOPED-VISIBILITY` during the live-docs pass, this would have been wrongly reported as unsupported — in the packet where it matters most.

I also flagged that the field has **no approvals by design** (*"the card rules ARE the policy"*), which makes the weekly exceptions report the only review step in the entire field programme — and that report has no configuration surface in Ramp. Worth stating so a reader doesn't mistake the absence for an oversight.

**NOTES.md is the only deliverable left.** I have five verification-delta cases banked against the two required, plus the go-live handoff and the capability/question section still to write.

Prompt: Why are some political entities considered to be “states” and others are not? Consider 
two political entities: Catalonia and South Sudan. Catalonia declared independence from Spain in 
October 2017, but the declaration was suspended and the former Catalonian president was arrested 
in Italy on charges of sedition. South Sudan, on the other hand, was recognized as a sovereign state 
almost immediately, but has suffered from chronic instability since independence a decade ago. 
What treaties, agreements or customs would you point to in order to assess whether each of these 
political units  meets  or does  not meet  the traditional  criteria  for  statehood?  What political 
considerations might play a role? Consider the arguments for and against recognition in each case. 
Discuss the reasons why South Sudan was able to achieve recognition and is still recognized as a 
sovereign state while Catalonia continues to be unable to get this recognition. 
Response: Evaluating the Criteria for Establishing Internationally Recognized Statehood 
In eva luating political entitie s suc h a s Catalonia and S outh Suda n and the ir claims on 
statehood, the Montevide o Conventi on appea rs to be the weake st framew ork by whic h any 
evaluation can be conducted. This traditional analysis of statehood - Article 1 of the Montevideo 
Convention on Rights and Duties of States (1933) - states: “The State as a person of international 
law should possess the following qualifications: (a) a permanent population; (b) a defined territory; 
(c
) government; and (d) capacity t o enter into relations with other States.’’1
Its language is still found in prese nt day commitments to internationa l law a nd is, to a 
certain degree, relevant. For example, the United Nati ons used the Mil lenium Declaration as an 
opportunity to rededicate its “support of upholding sovereign equality of all states by respect of 
their territory and political (governmental) independence.”2 However, through this paper, I attempt 
to move away from assessing statehood in the manner that Article 1 does. That is, the definition 
of statehood  as suggested by this  Convention assumes a tone of unification  (“permanent,” 
“defined,” “a government”) a nd in doing so leaves little room for non-dominant political parties 
power struggles, the weight of domestic a nd international interests, and can qualify statehood to 
1 Robert H. Jackson. “Quasi-States, Dual Regimes, and Neoclassical Theory: International Jurisprudence and the Third World 
(1987).” Edited by Beth A. Simmons and Richard  H. Steinberg. International Law and International Relations, n.d., 205–32. 
https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511808760.013.  
2 Tarcisio Gazzini and Robert Kolb. “The Autonomous Community of Catalonia and International Law. Swiss Review of 
International and European Law, 1-21. (2021) 

===== PAGE 2 =====
 
political entities that mirror the functions of states but are not interested in secession. This paper 
focuses instead on frameworks that highlight the strength of different political interests in 
discussing why Catalonia and South Sudan have varied outcomes on their status as a sovereign, 
state political entity.  
 
Catalonia: A Failed Case of Pursuing Statehood  
Negative Sovereignty: A Weak Argument for Catalonia’s Statehood 
 The custom of basing statehood on negative sovereignty offers, to a limited extent, a legal 
framework through which Catalonia’s proposition of self-determination and independence can be 
justified. A juridical statehood deriving itself from negative sovereignty constructs a statehood that 
is free through and has a right to self -determination.3 This type of statehood is a popular, period -
appropriate definition given current beliefs “in the inherent equality of all peoples regardless of 
their empirical capabilities and credibilities as organi zed political systems.” 4 Catalan authorities 
have a history of using language fitting of this custom. In 2012, Catalan authorities claimed a “right 
to decide” and “announced Catalonia as «a new State of Europe», based on the imprescriptible and 
inalienable right to self-determination as democratic expression of its sovereignty as nation.”5 This 
continues in 2017 as the Catalan Parliament organizes a controversial referendum on self -
determination.6

(1987).” Edited by Beth A. Simmons and Richard  H. Steinberg. International Law and International Relations, n.d., 205–32. 
https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511808760.013.  
4 Ibid., 205-32 
5 Tarcisio Gazzini and Robert Kolb. “The Autonomous Community of Catalonia and International Law. Swiss Review of

the Millenium Declaration,” ...the right to self -determination of peoples which remain under 
colonial domination and foreign occupation...” 7 This declaration suggests that self-determination

determination.9

cat > NOTES.md <<'MDEOF'
# NOTES

Five packets, each passing nine checks. What follows is what I decided, what I got wrong,
and how I found out. Commit hashes are the session pointers — the repository history is
the transcript.

## The audit log is the deliverable; the config is downstream of it

The exercise says the audit log is half the deliverable. I treated that as an ordering
constraint rather than a sentiment: Phase 2 writes `audit_log.json` **before** Phase 3
writes the config (`3203145`). Composing first and documenting afterwards produces an
audit log that rationalises a config already written. Flagging first forces the config to
be the consequence of the flags.

The alternative I passed on was the obvious one — compose, then annotate. It is faster and
it reads the same. It is also how a confidently wrong config gets a confident audit log.

## Verdicts derived from an OpenAPI snapshot are weaker evidence than they look

I built the capability ledger in two deliberate passes so the difference between them
would be visible. Pass 1 (`ab1f6db`) took every verdict from the 2026-08-30 snapshot
alone, and I asserted in code that no row cited anything else. Pass 2 (`86be791`) checked
the same rows against live documentation.

Every correction ran the same direction: the snapshot-only pass **over-claimed that Ramp
could not do things it can**. Absence of an endpoint is not evidence of absence of a
capability — it is evidence about an API surface. That distinction is the single most
useful thing I learned here, and `git diff ab1f6db 86be791` is the record of it.

I rejected keeping the ledger as prose. Machine-readable rows let the false-positive and
false-negative sweeps run as mechanical checks rather than as my own judgement about my
own work.

## The unit of the ledger is a customer request, not an endpoint

Forty-three rows, keyed on things customers say — "the card must decline for this vendor",
"I never want to see a decline" — not on API paths. This is what made packets cheaper as
the set went on: the same rows fired across all five. Keying on endpoints would have
produced a reference nobody consults while reading a transcript.

## Enforcement beats intention

Every rule that mattered ended up as a check in `run_pipeline.py --verify`, because the
rules I merely wrote down are the rules I personally broke. The pronoun rule, the
no-invented-identifier rule, and the name-placeholder rule were each violated by text I
wrote *after* writing the rule. Nine checks now gate every packet; a fully green run is
also the only thing that writes `deliverables/`.

# Verification delta

**The ledger told Vanguard's district managers they could not be served.** Pass 1 marked
`CAP-SCOPED-VISIBILITY` UNSUPPORTED, reasoning from `GET /roles` being read-only: no
custom roles, therefore no scoping. Ramp's *User roles overview* says visibility follows
the **management chain**, not department labels — and that chain is settable through the
API via `direct_manager_id`. Verdict corrected to PARTIAL (`86be791`). Packet E asks for
exactly this: six district managers seeing only their own district. Uncorrected, I would
have reported a supported requirement as impossible, in the packet where it matters most.

**My coverage invariant was hollow.** The pipeline's central promise is that every
extracted requirement terminates in a config field or an audit entry. Testing it against
the Westbrook sample's real outputs, the check passed while my fixture cited
`assumptions_made[999]` against an array with one entry (`ae90065`). Nothing resolved
citations against the document. "Everything lands somewhere" means nothing if the
somewhere need not exist. I added a resolution check, which immediately caught two more
dangling references I had written myself.

Three others, briefly: the category vocabulary is 43 codes, not the 44 I had inherited and
repeated in four places (`15e188f`); a `.title()` normaliser turned `IT` into `It`,
orphaning a user from the department the same config creates — both valid strings, so
schema validation passed (`9549f2f`); and both CEOs held administrative rights nobody
granted, in Hypergrowth's case against an explicit statement that the CEO should *not* be
making account changes (`29059cd`).

# What the Ramp documentation changed

`docs.ramp.com` and `ramp.com` were blocked by this environment's egress proxy for both
`curl` and page fetches. WebSearch was the only live channel, so what follows rests on
page titles and quoted excerpts, not full pages — worth stating plainly rather than
implying deeper reading.

- **Entities** — the accounting guide states it positively: *"Entities are created in the
  Ramp UI, and objects are scoped to an `entity_id` when fetching via the API."* This moved
  `CAP-ENTITY-CREATE` from an absence-based UNSUPPORTED to an evidenced UI_ONLY, and
  validated packet B's `status: requested`.
- **Roles** — *User roles overview* and *User role deep-dive: IT Admin* supply semantics the
  spec does not. `IT_ADMIN` grants People and Integrations access while explicitly denying
  spend controls, which is precisely the "manage users but not limits" split Acme and
  Hypergrowth both asked for. The enum value alone tells you nothing.
- **Approvals** — *Set up your spend approval policies* documents a workflow builder inside
  the application. The chain is real; only the API surface is missing. UI_ONLY, not
  unsupported.
- **Categories** — *Setting up category and merchant restrictions* confirms Ramp derives its
  own category from the MCC plus other signals. An MCC allow-list is therefore not
  expressible anywhere in the product, UI included — which is the whole of packet E's
  problem.
- **Naming** — the docs still title the resource *Creating spend limits* while the snapshot
  path is `/developer/v1/funds`, with both `limits:*` and `funds:*` scopes defined. The
  concept exists under a different path; claiming otherwise would have been the easiest
  wrong answer in the set.

# Go-live handoff — Apex Health Partners

For the deployment owner, before go-live:

- **REQ-3 is not met as written and Compliance has to see that in those words.** Ramp cannot
  check a purchase order while a card is being authorised — no platform does this at
  authorisation time. What is configured instead is the control your own document provides
  for: hard per-transaction caps, same-day reconciliation against NetSuite, and card
  suspension on violation. That is detective, not preventive, and your document reserves
  the right to *review* such a control rather than accept it in advance.
- **There is a $500 gap between your two documents that neither mentions.** The compliance
  document requires a purchase order above $500; the discovery call sets the clinic
  per-transaction cap at $1,000. A $700 clinic purchase is approved by the card and falls
  inside the purchase-order rule. Configured at $1,000 so clinics can operate — Compliance
  needs to accept reconciliation as the control for that band, or lower the cap.
- **REQ-2 fails closed, but a person is the gate.** High-limit cards are created and
  immediately suspended, and stay suspended until your office confirms the notarised form.
  A card left alone never transacts. Ramp does not verify the form exists; the Compliance
  Office does.
- **REQ-1 needs one thing from you before it works.** Both trading names — Joe's Medical
  Supply and JMS Distribution — must resolve to merchant records in Ramp. Any name that does
  not resolve is not blocked. The block also has to be re-applied to every programme created
  later, because Ramp has no company-wide blocklist.
- **Nothing can be issued until the roster arrives.** Eight blocking questions are open, and
  the largest is that this packet contains no email address for anyone and no clinic manager
  is named. The three-week clinic go-live starts when that list does.

# One capability, one question

**Capability: the ledger itself.** Every packet asked the same forty-odd questions — can
Ramp block a vendor, expire a card, scope a manager's view, allow-list an MCC — and the
answers do not vary by customer. Genera should own that ledger centrally, with dated
evidence per row and a regeneration step, so no deployment re-derives it and no two
customers get different answers to the same question. Its value compounds: the rows written
for Acme answered Apex, and rows added for Apex answered Vanguard.

**Question, for Vanguard Retail Services:** the seasonal wave is not a one-off. The field
force roughly doubles every October and collapses on 24 December, and the reps live in a
spreadsheet that is rebuilt each year. Should this become a standing annual motion — a
saved role-to-control mapping plus a re-runnable onboarding flow — rather than a
configuration rebuilt from scratch each season? The date does not move, and neither does
the shape of the work.

# With another day

Reconcile the ledger against the live OpenAPI specification at
`docs.ramp.com/openapi/developer-api.json`, which I could not reach; my drift rows rest on
a point-in-time snapshot. Write the Spanish executive summary Logística Globex asked for —
their board reads Spanish and the two JSON files cannot satisfy that. Build the reverse
check I do not have: today nothing catches a *silently widened* permission on a SUPPORTED
capability, which is how Cloud computing reached Hypergrowth's software card and how both
CEOs got administrative rights. And put the six district assignments into packet E, since
the reporting-chain mechanism that answers their hardest requirement cannot be built
without them.
MDEOF

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /root/.claude/skills/synced/30b55237-fa8d-4346-85f3-2e4db5465126_c02dae3c-ded5-4a8e-9d7d-dbec3ec9390e/notes

# NOTES.md: the decision and verification log

The write-up of **how the work was driven**, read side by side with the session export by
someone deciding whether the story matches the transcript. Not a summary of what was built —
the README does that. Its subject is the operator: what was decided, what was passed on,
where the work was wrong, and what caught it.

**The verification delta is the section that carries the document.** Anyone can describe what
they built. A write-up with no delta reads as one of two things: work that was never checked,
or checking that was not reported. Both are worse than the errors themselves.

This skill lives in `~/.claude/skills/notes` and runs locally. It reads your chat history, it
queries whatever repo you point it at, and it writes one file. Nothing is committed, nothing
is uploaded, and the skill itself does not belong in the repo it describes.

## Three rules

1. **Every claim points somewhere that resolves.** A turn number, a verbatim prompt, a commit,
   a path. `check_notes.py` verifies all four against the real transcript and the real repo.
2. **Never invent a pointer.** Not a timestamp, not a quoted prompt, not a "roughly halfway
   through". Read the position off `session_index.py` rather than estimating it — a phrase
   that disagrees with where the turn actually sits is a caught error, and rightly.
3. **Wrong means wrong.** The delta is about beliefs that turned out false, not tests that
   passed. "Added a check, it went green" is not a delta; "believed X, found Y, changed Z" is.

## Work it in this order

**1. Index the history.** The transcript is the primary source; memory is not.

```
python3 ~/.claude/skills/notes/scripts/session_index.py                  # the timeline
python3 ~/.claude/skills/notes/scripts/session_index.py --grep ledger --all
python3 ~/.claude/skills/notes/scripts/session_index.py --turn 14        # quote it exactly
```

`--project PATH` reads another project's history; `--file` reads exports directly. Several
sessions on one project are read as one continuous history, oldest first. The timeline is
where the Decisions section comes from: scan your own prompts for the moments where the work
changed direction, and note the turns where you interrupted or corrected — those are the ones
a reviewer is looking for.

**2. Pull exact references from the repo.** The transcript says when you decided something;
the repo says what it actually became. `git log --format='%h %ad %s' --date=format:'%Y-%m-%d %H:%M'`
for the timeline, `git show <hash>` for what a decision really changed as opposed to what it
was described as changing, `grep` for the line a claim rests on. Quote the repo, do not
paraphrase it from memory — the numbers move. Re-derive every count at write time.

**3. Write it. 4. Check it.** Both below.

## The shape the check enforces

Six `##` sections, in this order:

```
## Decisions
### 1. <the decision, as a claim>
**Passed on:** <the alternative actually considered, and why it lost>
**Where:** turn 14, about two-thirds in — "the exact words you used"

## Verification delta
### <short name of the error>
**Believed:** ...   **Evidence:** ...   **Change:** ...

## What the Ramp docs changed
## Go-live handoff — <Customer name>
## One capability, one question
## What I'd do next with another day
```

**The `**Where:**` line is the anchor, and it is parsed.** A `turn N` must exist; a position
phrase must match where that turn really sits (adjacent is close enough — prose is not graded
to three decimals); a quoted fragment on that line must appear verbatim in the history. Use
the phrases `session_index.py` prints: *at the very start, early on, about a third in, about
halfway, about two-thirds in, late on, right at the end.*

Where the work predates any transcript on this machine, anchor on a commit hash in backticks
instead and say plainly in the preamble that the pointers are commits. A commit is timestamped
and durable; a half-remembered "somewhere in the middle" is neither.

## Section by section

**Decisions (3–5).** A fork where a different reasonable person goes the other way. The test
is `**Passed on:**`: if no alternative was genuinely on the table, it is a description of what
got built, not a decision. Say what the alternative would have cost — "a fully scripted
extractor" is a real alternative; "doing it badly" is not. Order by how much of the work's
shape they explain, not chronologically.

**Verification delta (two minimum).** Prefer errors that a green test run would not have
caught, and prefer your own to the agent's — an operator who only reports the model's mistakes
has not looked hard at their own. If a check was added in response, name it: that is what
makes the fix durable rather than a one-off. If a search genuinely turned up nothing, say how
you looked — which files, which probes, what you expected to find — and expect scepticism.

**What the docs changed.** Only findings that changed an output. Cite the page as you would to
a colleague who has to find it again: site, page title, date checked. **State the access
constraint if there was one.** If the docs were reachable only through search snippets, saying
so is the difference between an honest citation and an implied deeper reading.

**Go-live handoff (exactly five bullets).** Written to a named person at the customer who will
forward it inside their company. Every bullet is something they must do, decide, or know
before go-live — not a description of your work. No internal vocabulary, no repo paths, no
turn numbers; the check rejects all three. Lead with what blocks go-live. If a control they
asked for is enforced by process rather than by the platform, that is a bullet.

**One capability, one question.** The capability is worth building once and using across
customers — test it against a case nobody has seen. Say what it costs and saves, and name the
runner-up you did not pick. The question is asked of one named customer and should be
answerable by them without doing your job for them.

**What I'd do next.** Ordered, with the reason each is next. Include the known-imperfect thing
you shipped anyway; a list of pure expansion, with nothing to repair, is not credible next to
a delta that found real errors.

## Length

At most two pages — the check fails above 1,300 words. It is a hard constraint and the
sections are not equally compressible. Cut in this order: the next-day list, then the
decisions (five to three), then the docs section. **Never cut the delta or the handoff.**
Expect this to cost real content; that is the constraint working, not a miscalibration.

## Check it

```
python3 ~/.claude/skills/notes/scripts/check_notes.py            # in the project directory
python3 ~/.claude/skills/notes/scripts/check_notes.py --notes path/to/NOTES.md --repo ~/code/thing
```

Seven checks: sections present and in order; length; every transcript pointer resolves
(turn exists, quote is real, position is honest); every commit hash and path resolves; 3–5
decisions each with an alternative and a pointer; two or more delta entries with belief,
evidence and change; a five-bullet handoff with no internal vocabulary or repo paths. An
`UNVERIFIED` result counts as a failure — unverified means the check did not happen.

The check reads structure, vocabulary and pointers. It cannot tell whether a decision was
real, whether an alternative was ever actually considered, or whether a delta entry is a
genuine error rather than a rounded-off one. Green is the floor, not the bar.

## Working notes

**When the history is partial.** Transcripts live on the machine that ran the session, so work
done in another container or another tool has none here. Anchor that work on commits, say so
once in the preamble, and do not fabricate the pointers you wish you had. Check (c) will tell
you how many turns it found and over what dates, which is usually enough to see immediately
that you are pointing at the wrong history.

**If a check fires on something the document genuinely needs, fix the check.** The customer's
own vocabulary outranks the jargon list. The one thing not to do is launder the sentence until
the check stops complaining.

**Scripts.** `session_index.py` (~250 lines) parses chat history; `check_notes.py` (~250)
verifies the document against it. Both are read-only, both are plain stdlib, and neither
writes anything.

# NOTES

Five packets, each passing nine checks. Pointers are turn numbers from this session's
transcript and commit hashes from this repository; the two together are the record.

## Decisions

### 1. The audit log is written before the config, not after it

Phase 2 emits `audit_log.json` before Phase 3 emits `ramp_config.json` (`3203145`).
Composing first and documenting afterwards produces an audit log that rationalises a
config already written; flagging first makes the config the consequence of the flags.

**Passed on:** compose, then annotate. Faster, and the output reads identically — which is
the problem. It is how a confidently wrong config acquires a confident audit log.

**Where:** turn 2, at the very start — "write SKILL.md, run_pipeline.py as a mix of glue code"

### 2. Judgement stays with the session; only the deterministic parts are code

`run_pipeline.py` inventories the packet and runs nine checks. Reading a messy transcript,
resolving a conflict and deciding what Ramp cannot do sit with the agent, guided by
`SKILL.md`. The split is the reason the pipeline handled five packets of different shapes.

**Passed on:** a scripted extractor. It would have worked on packet A's clean roster and
failed on packet D, which has no documents at all — only a Slack export and second-hand
notes that disagree.

**Where:** turn 2, at the very start — "such that a fresh Claude Code or Codex session can run any packet end-to-end"

### 3. The capability ledger is keyed on customer requests, not endpoints

Forty-three rows keyed on what customers say — "the card must decline for this vendor" —
each carrying a verdict, dated evidence and a workaround. Each packet was cheaper than the
last because the same rows fired across all five.

**Passed on:** an endpoint-keyed API reference. Accurate, and nobody opens it mid-transcript.

**Where:** turn 1, at the very start — "focusing on the capability ledger"

### 4. Every rule that mattered became a check, because I broke the ones I only wrote down

The pronoun rule, the no-invented-identifier rule and the name-placeholder rule were each
violated by text I wrote *after* writing the rule. Nine checks now gate every packet, and
only a fully green run writes `deliverables/`.

**Passed on:** documenting the standards in `SKILL.md` and relying on care. Measured on the
first audit log, care produced 36 pronoun violations and 17 unattributed citations.

**Where:** turn 7, early on — "Because this is customer facing, let's never write notes with"

## Verification delta

### The ledger told Vanguard's district managers they could not be served

**Believed:** `CAP-SCOPED-VISIBILITY` was UNSUPPORTED, reasoned from `GET /roles` being
read-only — no custom roles, therefore no scoping.

**Evidence:** Ramp's *User roles overview* states visibility follows the management chain,
not department labels, and that chain is settable through the API via `direct_manager_id`.

**Change:** verdict corrected to PARTIAL (`86be791`). Packet E asks precisely this — six
district managers seeing only their own district. Uncorrected, I would have reported a
supported requirement as impossible in the packet where it matters most. Every correction
in that pass ran the same direction: the snapshot-only reading over-claimed that Ramp could
not do things it can.

### The coverage invariant was hollow

**Believed:** the pipeline's central promise — every extracted requirement terminates in a
config field or an audit entry — was enforced.

**Evidence:** testing against the Westbrook sample's real outputs, the check passed while my
fixture cited `assumptions_made[999]` against an array holding one entry. Nothing resolved
citations against the document.

**Change:** added a reference-resolution check (`ae90065`), which immediately caught two
further dangling references I had written myself.

### Both CEOs held administrative rights nobody granted

**Believed:** an owner maps to `BUSINESS_ADMIN`, generalised from the Westbrook sample.

**Evidence:** Acme's administrators were named as "Priya and me"; Hypergrowth's as "me and
maya", with the stated reason for making the assistant an administrator being to keep
account changes away from the CEO. Neither CEO was in either list.

**Change:** both became `BUSINESS_USER`, and the ledger row now maps by administrative
responsibility rather than job title (`29059cd`). Found by re-reading A and C against a rule
derived from D — three others surfaced the same way, including a `.title()` normaliser that
turned `IT` into `It` and orphaned a user from the department the same config creates.

## What the Ramp docs changed

`docs.ramp.com` was blocked by this environment's egress proxy for both `curl` and page
fetches. Search was the only live channel, so these rest on page titles and quoted excerpts
rather than full pages.

- **Entities** — the accounting guide states it positively: entities are created in the Ramp
  UI and objects are scoped by `entity_id` when fetched. Moved `CAP-ENTITY-CREATE` from an
  absence-based UNSUPPORTED to an evidenced UI_ONLY, and validated packet B's
  `status: requested`.
- **Roles** — *User role deep-dive: IT Admin* supplies semantics the spec does not:
  `IT_ADMIN` grants People and Integrations access while denying spend controls. That is
  exactly the "manage users but not limits" split Acme and Hypergrowth both asked for.
- **Categories** — *Setting up category and merchant restrictions* confirms Ramp derives its
  category from the MCC plus other signals, so an MCC allow-list is not expressible anywhere
  in the product, UI included. That is the whole of packet E's problem.
- **Naming** — the docs still title the resource *Creating spend limits* while the snapshot
  path is `/developer/v1/funds`. The concept exists under another path; claiming otherwise
  would have been the easiest wrong answer in the set.

## Go-live handoff — Apex Health Partners

- **REQ-3 is not met as written, and Compliance should see it in those words.** Ramp cannot
  check a purchase order while a card is being authorised. What is configured instead is the
  control your own document provides for: hard per-transaction caps, same-day reconciliation
  against NetSuite, suspension on violation. That is detective, not preventive.
- **There is a $500 gap between your two documents that neither mentions.** Your compliance
  document requires a purchase order above $500; the discovery call sets the clinic
  per-transaction cap at $1,000. A $700 clinic purchase is approved by the card and falls
  inside the purchase-order rule. Accept reconciliation as the control for that band, or
  lower the cap.
- **The high-limit card gate fails closed, but a person is the gate.** Cards above $10,000 a
  month are created and immediately suspended, and stay suspended until your office confirms
  the notarised form. Ramp does not verify the form exists; the Compliance Office does.
- **The vendor block needs one thing from you before it works.** Both trading names, Joe's
  Medical Supply and JMS Distribution, must resolve to merchant records in Ramp. A name that
  does not resolve is not blocked. The block must also be re-applied to every card programme
  created later.
- **Nothing can be issued until the roster arrives.** Eight questions are open that stop
  go-live; the largest is that we have no email address for anyone and no clinic manager is
  named. Your three-week clinic timeline starts when that list does.

## One capability, one question

# NOTES

Five packets, nine checks each. Pointers are turn numbers from this session's transcript and
commit hashes from this repository.

## Decisions

### 1. The audit log is written before the config, not after it

Phase 2 emits `audit_log.json` before Phase 3 emits `ramp_config.json` (`3203145`). Composing
first and documenting after produces an audit log that rationalises a config already written,
whereas flagging first makes the config the consequence of the flags.

**Passed on:** compose, then annotate. Faster, and the output reads identically, which is
exactly the problem. It is how a confidently wrong config acquires a confident audit log.

**Where:** turn 2, at the very start — "write SKILL.md, run_pipeline.py as a mix of glue code"

### 2. Judgement stays with the session and only the deterministic parts are code

`run_pipeline.py` inventories the packet and runs nine checks. Reading a messy transcript,
resolving a conflict and deciding what Ramp cannot do stay with the agent, guided by
`SKILL.md`.

**Passed on:** a scripted extractor. It would have worked on packet A's clean roster but
failed on packet D, which has no documents at all, only a Slack export and second-hand notes
that disagree.

**Where:** turn 2, at the very start — "such that a fresh Claude Code or Codex session can run any packet end-to-end"

### 3. The capability ledger is keyed on customer requests, not endpoints

Forty-three rows keyed on what customers say, such as "the card must decline for this
vendor", each with a verdict, dated evidence and a workaround. Each packet was cheaper than
the last because the same rows fired across all five.

**Passed on:** an endpoint-keyed API reference. Accurate, but nobody opens one mid-transcript.

**Where:** turn 1, at the very start — "focusing on the capability ledger"

### 4. Every rule that mattered became a check, because I broke the ones I only wrote down

The pronoun rule, the no-invented-identifier rule and the name-placeholder rule were each
violated by text I wrote *after* writing the rule. Nine checks now gate every packet, and only
a fully green run writes `deliverables/`.

**Passed on:** documenting the standards and relying on care. Measured on the first audit log,
care produced 36 pronoun violations and 17 unattributed citations.

**Where:** turn 7, early on — "Because this is customer facing, let's never write notes with"

## Verification delta

### The ledger told Vanguard's district managers they could not be served

**Believed:** `CAP-SCOPED-VISIBILITY` was UNSUPPORTED, reasoned from `GET /roles` being
read-only, so no custom roles and therefore no scoping.

**Evidence:** *User roles overview* states visibility follows the management chain rather than
department labels, and that chain is settable via `direct_manager_id`.

**Change:** corrected to PARTIAL (`86be791`). Packet E asks precisely this, six district
managers seeing only their own district, so uncorrected I would have called a supported
requirement impossible in the packet where it matters most. Every correction in that pass ran
one way: the snapshot-only reading over-claimed what Ramp cannot do.

### The coverage invariant was hollow

**Believed:** the central promise, that every requirement terminates in a config field or an
audit entry, was enforced.

**Evidence:** against the Westbrook sample's real outputs the check passed while my fixture
cited `assumptions_made[999]` against an array holding one entry. Nothing resolved citations
against the document.

**Change:** added a reference-resolution check (`ae90065`), which immediately caught two
further dangling references I had written myself.

### Both CEOs held administrative rights nobody granted

**Believed:** an owner maps to `BUSINESS_ADMIN`, generalised from the Westbrook sample.

**Evidence:** Acme's administrators were named as "Priya and me" and Hypergrowth's as "me and
maya", the stated reason for the assistant being to keep account changes away from the CEO.
Neither CEO appeared in either list.

**Change:** both became `BUSINESS_USER`, and the ledger row now maps by administrative
responsibility rather than job title (`29059cd`). Found by re-reading A and C against a rule
derived from D. Three more surfaced the same way, including a `.title()` normaliser that
turned `IT` into `It` and orphaned a user from the department the same config creates.

## What the Ramp docs changed

`docs.ramp.com` was blocked by this environment's egress proxy for both `curl` and page
fetches. Search was the only live channel, so these rest on page titles and quoted excerpts
rather than full pages.

- **Entities.** The accounting guide states positively that entities are created in the Ramp
  UI and scoped by `entity_id` when fetched. This moved `CAP-ENTITY-CREATE` from absence-based
  UNSUPPORTED to evidenced UI_ONLY and validated packet B's `status: requested`.
- **Roles.** *User role deep-dive: IT Admin* supplies semantics the spec does not. `IT_ADMIN`
  grants People and Integrations access while denying spend controls, which is exactly the
  "manage users but not limits" split Acme and Hypergrowth both asked for.
- **Categories.** *Setting up category and merchant restrictions* confirms Ramp derives its
  category from the MCC plus other signals, so an MCC allow-list is not expressible anywhere in
  the product, UI included. That is the whole of packet E's problem.
- **Naming.** The docs still title the resource *Creating spend limits* while the snapshot path
  is `/developer/v1/funds`. Claiming the concept absent would have been the easiest wrong
  answer in the set.

## Go-live handoff — Apex Health Partners

- **REQ-3 is not met as written, and Compliance should see it in those words.** Ramp cannot
  check a purchase order while a card is being authorised. What is configured instead is the
  control your own document provides for: hard per-transaction caps, same-day reconciliation
  against NetSuite, and suspension on violation. That is detective rather than preventive.
- **There is a $500 gap between your two documents that neither mentions.** Your compliance
  document requires a purchase order above $500, while the discovery call sets the clinic
  per-transaction cap at $1,000. A $700 clinic purchase is approved by the card and still falls
  inside the purchase-order rule. Either accept reconciliation as the control for that band, or
  lower the cap.
- **The high-limit card gate fails closed, but a person is the gate.** Cards above $10,000 a
  month are created and immediately suspended, and stay suspended until your office confirms
  the notarised form. Ramp does not verify that the form exists. The Compliance Office does.

# NOTES

Five packets, nine checks each. Pointers are transcript turn numbers and commit hashes.

## Decisions

### 1. The audit log is written before the config, not after it

Phase 2 emits `audit_log.json` before Phase 3 emits `ramp_config.json` (`3203145`). Composing
first and documenting after produces an audit log that rationalises a config already written,
whereas flagging first makes the config a consequence of the flags.

**Passed on:** compose, then annotate. Faster, and the output reads identically, which is the
problem: it is how a confidently wrong config acquires a confident audit log.

**Where:** turn 2, at the very start — "write SKILL.md, run_pipeline.py as a mix of glue code"

### 2. Judgement stays with the session and only the deterministic parts are code

`run_pipeline.py` inventories the packet and runs nine checks. Reading a messy transcript,
resolving conflicts and deciding what Ramp cannot do stay with the agent.

**Passed on:** a scripted extractor. It would have worked on packet A's clean roster but failed
on packet D, which has no documents at all, only a Slack export and notes that disagree.

**Where:** turn 2, at the very start — "such that a fresh Claude Code or Codex session can run any packet end-to-end"

### 3. The capability ledger is keyed on customer requests, not endpoints

Forty-three rows keyed on what customers say, such as "the card must decline for this vendor",
each with a verdict, dated evidence and a workaround. Each packet was cheaper than the last.

**Passed on:** an endpoint-keyed API reference. Accurate, but nobody opens one mid-packet.

**Where:** turn 1, at the very start — "focusing on the capability ledger"

### 4. Every rule that mattered became a check, because I broke the ones I only wrote down

The pronoun rule, the no-invented-identifier rule and the name-placeholder rule were each
violated by text I wrote *after* writing the rule. Nine checks now gate every packet.

**Passed on:** documenting the standards and relying on care. Measured on the first audit log,
care produced 36 pronoun violations and 17 unattributed citations.

**Where:** turn 7, early on — "Because this is customer facing, let's never write notes with"

## Verification delta

### The ledger told Vanguard's district managers they could not be served

**Believed:** `CAP-SCOPED-VISIBILITY` was UNSUPPORTED, reasoned from `GET /roles` being
read-only: no custom roles, therefore no scoping.

**Evidence:** *User roles overview* states visibility follows the management chain, not
department labels, and that chain is settable via `direct_manager_id`.

**Change:** corrected to PARTIAL (`86be791`). Packet E asks precisely this, six district
managers seeing only their own district, so uncorrected I would have called a supported
requirement impossible where it matters most. Every correction in that pass ran one way: the
snapshot-only reading over-claimed what Ramp cannot do.

### The coverage invariant was hollow

**Believed:** the central promise, that every requirement terminates in a config field or audit
entry, was enforced.

**Evidence:** against the sample's real outputs the check passed while my fixture cited
`assumptions_made[999]` against an array holding one entry. Nothing resolved citations against
the document.

**Change:** added a reference-resolution check (`ae90065`), which immediately caught two more
dangling references I had written myself.

### Both CEOs held administrative rights nobody granted

**Believed:** an owner maps to `BUSINESS_ADMIN`, generalised from the Westbrook sample.

**Evidence:** Acme's administrators were named as "Priya and me" and Hypergrowth's as "me and
maya", the stated reason for the assistant being to keep account changes away from the CEO.
Neither CEO appeared in either list.

**Change:** both became `BUSINESS_USER`, and the ledger row now maps by administrative
responsibility rather than job title (`29059cd`). Found by re-reading A and C against a rule
derived from D. Three more surfaced the same way, including a `.title()` normaliser that turned
`IT` into `It`, orphaning a user from the department that same config creates.

## What the Ramp docs changed

`docs.ramp.com` was blocked by this environment's egress proxy for both `curl` and page
fetches. Search was the only live channel, so these rest on page titles and quoted excerpts
rather than full pages.

- **Entities.** The accounting guide states positively that entities are created in the Ramp UI
  and scoped by `entity_id`, moving `CAP-ENTITY-CREATE` from absence-based UNSUPPORTED to
  evidenced UI_ONLY and validating packet B's `status: requested`.
- **Roles.** *User role deep-dive: IT Admin* supplies semantics the spec does not: `IT_ADMIN`
  grants People and Integrations access while denying spend controls, exactly the "manage users
  but not limits" split Acme and Hypergrowth both asked for.
- **Categories.** *Setting up category and merchant restrictions* confirms Ramp derives its
  category from the MCC plus other signals, so an MCC allow-list is not expressible anywhere in
  the product, UI included. That is the whole of packet E's problem.
- **Naming.** The docs still title the resource *Creating spend limits* while the snapshot path
  is `/developer/v1/funds`. Calling the concept absent was the easiest wrong answer here.

## Go-live handoff — Apex Health Partners

- **REQ-3 is not met as written, and Compliance should see it in those words.** Ramp cannot
  check a purchase order while a card is being authorised. Configured instead is the control your
  own document provides for: hard per-transaction caps, same-day reconciliation against NetSuite,
  and suspension on violation. That is detective rather than preventive.
- **There is a $500 gap between your two documents that neither mentions.** Your compliance
  document requires a purchase order above $500, while the discovery call sets the clinic
  per-transaction cap at $1,000. A $700 purchase is approved by the card and still falls inside
  the purchase-order rule. Either accept reconciliation as the control for that band, or lower
  the cap.
- **The high-limit card gate fails closed, but a person is the gate.** Cards above $10,000 a
  month are created and immediately suspended, staying suspended until your office confirms the
  notarised form. Ramp does not verify that the form exists. The Compliance Office does.
- **The vendor block needs one thing from you before it works.** Both trading names, Joe's
  Medical Supply and JMS Distribution, must resolve to merchant records in Ramp, because a name
  that does not resolve is not blocked. The block must also be re-applied to every card programme
  created later.
- **Nothing can be issued until the roster arrives.** Eight open questions stop go-live, and the
  largest is that we have no email address for anyone and no clinic manager is named. Your
  three-week clinic timeline starts when that list does.

## One capability, one question

**Capability: the ledger, owned centrally.** Every packet asked the same forty-odd questions,
such as whether Ramp can block a vendor or allow-list an MCC, and the answers do not vary by
customer. Built once with dated evidence per row, it removes that re-derivation from every
deployment after: rows written for Acme answered Apex, and rows added for Apex answered
Vanguard. Runner-up was the audit-log style gate, which travels less well because it encodes one
house voice where the ledger encodes facts.

**Question, for Vanguard Retail Services:** your field force roughly doubles every October and
collapses on 24 December, and the reps live in a spreadsheet rebuilt each year. Should the
seasonal wave become a standing annual motion, with a saved role-to-control mapping and a
re-runnable onboarding flow, rather than rebuilt each season?

## What I'd do next with another day

Reconcile the ledger against the live OpenAPI specification I could not reach, since every
drift row rests on a snapshot and drift ages worst. Then build the check I lack: nothing catches
a silently widened permission on a SUPPORTED capability, which is how Cloud computing reached
Hypergrowth's software card and how both CEOs got administrative rights, all caught by reading
rather than tooling. Then the Spanish executive summary Logística Globex asked for. Shipped
knowingly imperfect: packet C's clinic programme permits General merchandise as the nearest
category to "hardware stores", broader than that packet deserves.

**No, the skill does not account for writing style.** It governs structure (six sections in a fixed order), pointer discipline, the 1,300-word ceiling, and forbidden vocabulary in the handoff. content.text:
Confirmed a real hazard: deleting an audit entry shifts every later `audit_refs` index and stays in range, so no existing check would catch it. That shapes Agent 3's constraints.

Two forks I don't want to guess at.

questions.question: The exercise README explicitly says to study the sample for output shapes and audit-log idioms, so some resemblance is intended. What should count as contamination to remove?

options.label: Unearned inheritance only (Recommended)
options.description: Remove sample-derived content, values, or reasoning that was NOT re-derived from the packet's own sources — e.g. the owner→BUSINESS_ADMIN mapping, 'pending roster' where no roster exists. Keep deliberate idiom adoption the README asks for: evidence-line format, omit-and-flag, source quotes, tier-0 AUTO.

options.label: Also re-derive every shared idiom
options.description: Additionally justify each structural idiom against the packet itself, and drop any that only exist because the sample did it. More thorough, but risks diverging from the graded example and making outputs worse for no evidential gain.

options.label: Audit and report only, change nothing
options.description: Run agents 1 and 2, produce the findings, and stop before editing. You review the flag list and decide what gets applied. Safest, but leaves any real contamination in place for now.

questions.question: How much latitude should the implementing agent have when it hits a judgement call rather than a clear-cut fix?

options.label: Mechanical only, escalate judgement (Recommended)
options.description: Agent 3 applies findings that are evidence-backed and unambiguous (a value with no source, a placeholder asserting a document that doesn't exist). Anything needing a judgement call comes back to you with both options rather than being decided silently.

options.label: Full authority to resolve everything
options.description: Agent 3 applies every finding agent 2 flags, including judgement calls, documenting each in the audit log. Fastest to a finished state, but bakes in decisions you haven't seen — which is how the CEO-admin and Cloud-computing errors happened.

options.label: Propose diffs, apply nothing
options.description: Agent 3 writes the exact changes as a patch file for your review without touching out/. You apply them yourself. Maximum control, but adds a round trip before anything is green again.

That risk is not hypothetical. Three sample-derived errors have already been found and fixed during this build: - owner mapped to `BUSINESS_ADMIN`, generalised from Westbrook's Priti, which handed both Acme's and Hypergrowth's CEOs admin rights nobody granted (`29059cd`) - `"(surname pending roster)"` used for Apex Health, a packet with no roster, pending or otherwise (`85d83cf`) - the sample's `reimbursements_enabled: false` default, which the sample got right and which I departed from on three Apex programmes (`29059cd`) Each was caught by reading rather than by a check, and each was found only because something else prompted a re-read. This pass is the systematic version. **Preliminary read-only checks already run.** No literal leakage: zero occurrences of `westbrook`, `Priti`, `Nora`, `Studio`, or the sample's `2026-08-24` evidence date anywhere in `out/`. The sample's non-canonical category spelling `Software / SaaS` appears nowhere; all five packets use the API-canonical `SaaS / Software`. The separation is the point: the reviewer cannot rationalise because it does not judge, and the implementer cannot re-litigate because it does not classify. Intermediates go in `work/_sample_audit/`, which is outside `out/`. ### Agent 1 — Reviewer (read-only, no verdicts) Catalogues every point of contact between the sample and the five outputs. Does **not** decide whether any of it is a problem. Four dimensions: 1. **Literal content** — names, domains, dates, department names, category spellings, evidence strings. 2. **Structural idioms** — `approval_policies[].source` carrying a quote, tier-0 `AUTO`, omit-and-flag, name placeholders, group-cardinality notes, evidence-line shape, workaround naming a route, `conflicts: []`. 3. **Reasoning inheritance** — role mappings, and defaults chosen where a packet is *silent* (reimbursements, card type, receipt and memo omission). Silence is where inheritance hides. 4. **Value provenance** — every money value in every config traced to its own packet using `scripts/money_map.py`, which handles spelled-out amounts. A naive digit grep produces false positives here: packet C writes "twenty-five hundred" and "Fifteen hundred", packet B writes `R$ 6.000`.
